concepts.title: Upper vs. lower airway structures
key_points: The upper airway runs from the nose and mouth to the larynx: nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx, and larynx
The lower airway runs from the trachea down: trachea, carina, right and left mainstem bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap that covers the glottic opening during swallowing to keep food out of the trachea
The larynx (voice box) contains the vocal cords; the glottic opening between them is the narrowest part of the adult airway
The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway; the cricothyroid membrane sits just above it
The tongue is the most common cause of airway obstruction in an unresponsive patient because it relaxes back against the posterior pharynx
Gas exchange happens only in the alveoli; everything above them is a conducting passage
misconceptions: Thinking the trachea is part of the upper airway
Believing gas exchange happens in the bronchi
Forgetting that the tongue, not a foreign body, is the usual obstruction in the unresponsive patient
exam_favorites: Where the upper airway ends and the lower airway begins (the larynx / trachea boundary)
Function of the epiglottis
The tongue as the most common airway obstruction
The only complete cartilage ring (cricoid)

read.plain:
Air has one job on the way in: reach the alveoli, the millions of tiny sacs deep in the lungs where oxygen crosses into the blood. Everything between the nose and those sacs is just a hallway. Your job as an EMT is to keep the hallway open.

The upper airway is everything above the voice box. Air enters through the nose and mouth, passes through the pharynx (the throat), and reaches the larynx. The pharynx has three sections named for what sits in front of them: the nasopharynx behind the nose, the oropharynx behind the mouth, and the laryngopharynx just above the larynx. At the entrance to the larynx sits the epiglottis, a leaf-shaped flap that flips down when you swallow so food goes to the esophagus, not the lungs.

The larynx holds the vocal cords. The gap between them is the glottic opening, and in an adult it is the narrowest point in the whole airway. Just below the larynx is the cricoid cartilage, the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. Everything else is C-shaped and open at the back.

The lower airway starts at the trachea, the windpipe. It runs down to a fork called the carina, where it splits into the right and left mainstem bronchi, one to each lung. Those branch again and again into smaller bronchioles until they end at the alveoli, where the actual work of breathing happens.

One structure deserves special attention: the tongue. In an unresponsive patient lying on their back, the tongue relaxes and falls against the back of the throat. That is the number one cause of airway obstruction you will see, and it is why the first airway skills you learn are simply about moving the tongue out of the way.
read.standard:
The airway is divided at the larynx. The upper airway consists of the nasal cavity, oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx. The pharynx is subdivided into the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx (hypopharynx). The nasal passages warm, filter, and humidify inspired air. The epiglottis, a leaf-shaped cartilage at the base of the tongue, occludes the glottic opening during swallowing to protect the lower airway from aspiration.

The larynx houses the vocal cords; the glottic opening between them is the narrowest point of the adult airway. The thyroid cartilage forms the anterior prominence of the larynx. Immediately inferior is the cricoid cartilage, the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway. The cricothyroid membrane lies between the two and is the site for surgical airway access at the advanced level.

The lower airway begins at the trachea, which descends to the carina at approximately the level of the sternal angle and bifurcates into the right and left mainstem bronchi. The right mainstem is wider and more vertical, which is why aspirated material and misplaced tubes more often enter the right lung. The bronchi divide into progressively smaller bronchioles ending in alveolar sacs, where gas exchange occurs across the alveolar-capillary membrane.

In the unresponsive supine patient, loss of muscle tone allows the tongue to fall posteriorly against the pharyngeal wall, producing the most common form of airway obstruction. Basic positioning maneuvers correct this by displacing the mandible and tongue anteriorly.

eli_new.analogy: The airway is a tree upside down: the trunk is the trachea, the branches are the bronchi, and the leaves are the alveoli.
eli_new.body:
Above the trunk is the entrance: nose, mouth, throat, and a gate called the larynx. The epiglottis is the lid on that gate. When you swallow it closes so your sandwich goes down the other pipe.

Below the gate is the tree. Trunk (trachea), first two branches (bronchi), thousands of twigs (bronchioles), and finally the leaves (alveoli). Only the leaves do photosynthesis, and only the alveoli do gas exchange. The rest is plumbing.

The tongue is a wet sponge sitting at the entrance. Stand up and it stays put. Lie an unconscious person flat and the sponge slumps backward and blocks the door. That single fact is why airway management starts with tilting a head.

story.title: Snoring is not sleeping
story.dispatch: Rescue 4, 24-year-old male, unresponsive, possible overdose, friends on scene.
story.body:
He is flat on his back on the kitchen floor, and from the doorway you hear it: a wet, rattling snore with every breath. His friends think he is sleeping it off. You know what that sound is. It is his tongue, slumped back against his throat, letting only a sliver of air past.

You kneel, tilt his head back, and lift his chin. The snore stops instantly and his chest rises clean and quiet. Nothing else has changed; you just moved the sponge out of the doorway. Your partner reaches for an airway adjunct to hold it there while you get the rest of the assessment going. The friends are staring. 'That's it?' one of them asks. For the next thirty seconds, yes. That is it.

Then LOWER: trachea, carina, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli

concepts.title: Pediatric airway differences
key_points: Children have a proportionally larger tongue in a smaller mouth, so the tongue obstructs the airway more easily
A large occiput (back of the head) flexes the neck forward when the child lies flat; pad under the shoulders to keep the airway neutral
The airway is smaller and narrower overall, so a little swelling or a small object causes a big obstruction
The narrowest point in a young child is at the cricoid ring, not the vocal cords, giving the airway a funnel shape
The larynx sits higher and more anterior, and the epiglottis is floppier and more U-shaped
The trachea is soft and easily kinked; hyperextending the neck can close the airway rather than open it
Children have a higher metabolic rate and less reserve, so they become hypoxic faster than adults
Infants rely on the diaphragm to breathe and are preferential nose breathers for the first months of life
misconceptions: Tilting a child's head back as far as an adult's (hyperextension kinks the soft trachea)
Assuming a child can tolerate hypoxia as long as an adult can
Laying an infant flat on a hard surface and expecting a neutral airway
exam_favorites: Why you pad under an infant's shoulders
Narrowest point of the pediatric airway (cricoid)
Proportionally larger tongue and occiput
Why children desaturate faster

read.plain:
A child is not a small adult, and nowhere is that more true than the airway. Almost every difference works against you, so you need to know them cold.

Start with the tongue. A child's tongue is big for the size of the mouth, so it blocks the airway even more easily than an adult's. Then the head: a young child's skull is large in the back, so when you lay them flat the big occiput tips the head forward and bends the neck, folding the airway. The fix is to slide a folded towel under the shoulders, which brings the head back to a neutral position with the ear canal level with the shoulder.

The whole airway is smaller and narrower. That matters because obstruction is about area. A millimeter of swelling that an adult would never notice can cut a toddler's airway in half. The narrowest point is also different: in an adult it is the vocal cords, but in a young child it is the cricoid ring below them, so the airway is shaped like a funnel.

The larynx sits higher and further forward, and the epiglottis is floppy and shaped like a U, which can make things harder to see for advanced providers. The trachea is soft. If you crank a child's head back the way you might an adult's, you can kink that soft tube shut. Keep the tilt gentle; neutral for infants, only slightly extended for children.

Finally, children burn oxygen fast and have almost no reserve. An adult who stops breathing has a few minutes of stored oxygen. A child has far less. When a child's breathing goes bad, you act now.
read.standard:
Pediatric airway anatomy differs from adult anatomy in ways that increase the risk of obstruction and complicate management. The tongue is proportionally larger relative to the oral cavity, and the occiput is proportionally larger, which flexes the cervical spine when the child is supine. Padding beneath the shoulders in infants and small children restores a neutral position, with the external auditory canal aligned with the anterior shoulder.

All airway diameters are smaller, so equivalent degrees of edema or foreign material produce disproportionately greater resistance to airflow. The larynx is positioned higher and more anteriorly, the epiglottis is longer, softer, and more omega-shaped, and the narrowest point of the airway is at the cricoid cartilage rather than at the glottis, producing a funnel-shaped configuration until roughly age 8 to 10.

The trachea has less cartilaginous support and is more compliant, so hyperextension or hyperflexion of the neck can occlude it; the head-tilt/chin-lift is performed with only slight extension in children and a neutral position in infants. Infants are preferential nasal breathers and depend heavily on diaphragmatic excursion; gastric distention from aggressive ventilation impairs breathing significantly.

Because metabolic rate and oxygen consumption are higher and functional residual capacity is lower, children desaturate rapidly during apnea or hypoventilation. Respiratory compromise is the leading cause of cardiac arrest in children, which is why early airway and ventilation support are the priority in pediatric resuscitation.

eli_new.analogy: A child's airway is a drinking straw; an adult's is a garden hose. Pinch each one the same amount and see which stops flowing.
eli_new.body:
Everything about the pediatric airway is a smaller, softer, more crowded version of the adult one. The tongue is too big for the room. The head is too big for the neck, so lying flat bends the straw. The straw itself is thin, so a little swelling closes it, and it is soft, so bending the neck too far pinches it.

And the kid is running the engine at high RPM with a tiny gas tank. Adults coast for minutes without oxygen; children run out almost immediately. Every difference says the same thing: be gentle with the position, and be fast with the fix.

teach.prompt: Explain to a new EMT why you position a child's airway differently from an adult's.

Soft trachea; do not hyperextend

teach.model_answer: A child's head is big in the back, so lying flat tips the head forward and folds the airway. You pad under the shoulders to bring the head neutral. Then you do not tilt the head back very far, because the trachea is soft and hyperextending can kink it shut. And because the tongue is big and the airway is narrow, it obstructs easily, so you keep a close watch and fix problems fast, because kids run out of oxygen quickly.

story.title: The folded towel
story.dispatch: Engine 2, Rescue 2, 9-month-old, not breathing normally after a fall, mother on scene.
story.body:
The infant is on the living room floor, limp, making slow gurgling breaths. Mom is frantic. You go to lay the baby on the stretcher and your partner, who has kids, catches your hand. 'Wait.' She folds a towel into a flat square and slides it under the baby's shoulders. The head, which had been tipped forward with the chin nearly on the chest, settles back level. The gurgling eases.

You hold a gentle neutral position, no tilt, and get the bag-valve-mask on. The chest rises with each squeeze. Later, on the way in, your partner explains the towel. 'That big head bends the neck. Flat on a board, you've folded the straw. The towel unfolds it.' You will never put an infant on a flat surface again without reaching for a towel first.

concepts.title: Ventilation, respiration, and oxygenation
key_points: Ventilation is the mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs
Respiration is the exchange of gases: external respiration at the alveoli (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out of the blood) and internal respiration at the cells
Oxygenation is the loading of oxygen onto hemoglobin and delivery to tissues
A patient can be ventilating (moving air) and still not be oxygenating (for example, carbon monoxide poisoning or a lung full of fluid)
A patient can be oxygenating at the moment and still be failing to ventilate (carbon dioxide builds up when breathing is too slow or shallow)
Tidal volume is the air moved in one breath (about 500 mL in an adult); minute volume = tidal volume × respiratory rate
Dead space is air that never reaches the alveoli (about 150 mL); shallow breaths waste a larger share on dead space
Inhalation is active (diaphragm and intercostals contract); normal exhalation is passive
The drive to breathe is normally triggered by rising carbon dioxide, sensed in the brainstem
misconceptions: Using 'breathing' to mean all three things at once and missing which one has failed
Assuming chest rise means the patient is oxygenating
Thinking a normal pulse ox proves the patient is ventilating adequately
exam_favorites: Definitions of ventilation vs. respiration vs. oxygenation
Minute volume calculation
Why shallow breathing is so inefficient (dead space)
Carbon dioxide as the normal breathing stimulus

read.plain:
Three words get used as if they mean the same thing, and the exam will test whether you know they do not.

Ventilation is moving air. Chest rises, chest falls, air goes in and out. That is all ventilation means. A bag-valve-mask ventilates. It says nothing about whether any oxygen is getting into the blood.

Respiration is the swap. At the alveoli, oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out. That is external respiration. Out at the cells the reverse happens, oxygen off the blood and into the cell, carbon dioxide out; that is internal respiration.

Oxygenation is getting oxygen onto the hemoglobin in red blood cells and delivering it to the tissues. Pulse oximetry tries to measure this.

Why does the distinction matter? Because they fail separately. A carbon monoxide victim may be ventilating beautifully, chest rising, air flowing, and not oxygenating at all because CO has hijacked the hemoglobin. A patient breathing 6 shallow times a minute may still show a decent oxygen reading for a little while, but they are not ventilating enough, and carbon dioxide is piling up in the blood. When you assess breathing, ask which of the three is broken.

A couple of numbers help. One normal adult breath moves about 500 mL of air; that is tidal volume. Multiply it by the breaths per minute and you get minute volume, the total air moved per minute. But about 150 mL of every breath just fills the hallway, the trachea and bronchi, and never reaches the alveoli. That is dead space. If a patient takes tiny 200 mL breaths, 150 of every 200 is wasted. Shallow breathing is far worse than the rate alone suggests.

Last piece: what makes you breathe at all. Normally it is rising carbon dioxide, sensed by the brainstem. When CO2 climbs, you breathe faster. Oxygen level is a backup trigger that only takes over in some chronic lung patients.
read.standard:
Ventilation is the mechanical process of moving air into and out of the lungs, driven by pressure changes from contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles during inhalation and passive elastic recoil during normal exhalation. Respiration is gas exchange: external respiration across the alveolar-capillary membrane and internal respiration between systemic capillaries and tissue cells, both occurring by diffusion along concentration gradients. Oxygenation refers to the binding of oxygen to hemoglobin and its delivery to tissues.

These processes are assessed separately because they fail independently. Impaired ventilation (hypoventilation) causes carbon dioxide retention and respiratory acidosis even when oxygenation is transiently preserved. Impaired diffusion or hemoglobin dysfunction (pulmonary edema, carbon monoxide poisoning) causes hypoxia despite adequate ventilation. Impaired perfusion (shock, pulmonary embolism) prevents delivery even when both ventilation and alveolar gas exchange are intact.

Tidal volume in a resting adult is approximately 500 mL. Minute volume equals tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate; normal is roughly 6 to 8 L/min. Anatomic dead space, air remaining in conducting airways that does not participate in gas exchange, is approximately 150 mL. Alveolar ventilation therefore equals (tidal volume − dead space) × rate, which is why rapid shallow breathing can produce a normal-appearing minute volume with markedly reduced effective ventilation.

The primary respiratory drive is regulated by central chemoreceptors in the medulla responding to arterial CO2 and pH. Peripheral chemoreceptors responsive to low oxygen provide a secondary, hypoxic drive that becomes clinically relevant primarily in patients with chronic CO2 retention.

eli_new.analogy: Ventilation is the delivery truck, respiration is unloading at the dock, oxygenation is the cargo actually arriving at the stores.
eli_new.body:
The truck can run all day (chest rising and falling) and deliver nothing if the dock is flooded (fluid in the lungs) or the cargo is fake (carbon monoxide on the hemoglobin). That is ventilating without oxygenating. Or the trucks can be running too rarely and too small, so garbage (carbon dioxide) piles up at the stores even though today's shelves still look stocked. That is failing to ventilate while oxygenation looks fine for now.

Dead space is the part of the truck bed that always stays empty. A big truck (500 mL) with 150 mL of empty bed is fine. A tiny truck (200 mL) with the same 150 mL of empty bed barely delivers anything. Shallow breaths are tiny trucks.

do.prompt: A patient breathes 24 times a minute with a tidal volume of 250 mL. Dead space is 150 mL. What is the effective alveolar ventilation per minute?

config.worked_solution: (250 − 150) × 24 = 100 × 24 = 2,400 mL/min. Compare a normal adult: (500 − 150) × 12 = 4,200 mL/min. Breathing twice as fast still moves far less useful air.

teach.model_answer: Ventilation is just moving air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the gas exchange, oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out at the alveoli, and the reverse at the cells. story.title: Chest rise is not the finish line
story.dispatch: Medic 9, 52-year-old male, found unresponsive in a running car in a closed garage.
story.body:
Fire has already pulled him out. He is breathing, maybe 14 times a minute, chest rising evenly, color surprisingly pink. The rookie says 'his breathing's fine.' You put him on a non-rebreather at 15 anyway and start toward the truck, because you know what a closed garage means.

In the back you explain it. He is ventilating: air is moving. He is probably even respiring: gas is crossing at the alveoli. But he is not oxygenating, because carbon monoxide is sitting on his hemoglobin and the oxygen has nowhere to bind. The pink skin and the normal chest rise are both lying. The pulse ox will lie too. All three words look fine on the surface, and one of them is broken underneath. That is why you never stop at 'his breathing's fine.'

concepts.title: Normal breathing: rate, depth, and effort by age
key_points: Normal adult respiratory rate: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
Normal child (1 to 12 years) respiratory rate: about 15 to 30 breaths per minute
Normal infant (under 1 year) respiratory rate: about 25 to 50 breaths per minute
Normal breathing is regular in rhythm, adequate in depth (visible, equal chest rise), quiet, and effortless
No accessory muscle use, no retractions, no nasal flaring, and the patient can speak in full sentences
Count respirations for 30 seconds and multiply by 2; do not tell the patient you are counting or the rate will change
Rate alone is not adequacy: a patient breathing 16 times a minute with shallow breaths may still be ventilating inadequately
misconceptions: Memorizing only the adult range and applying it to children
Telling the patient 'I'm going to count your breathing' (they will change it)
Treating a normal rate as proof of adequate breathing without looking at depth and effort
exam_favorites: Normal respiratory rate ranges for adult, child, and infant
Signs that define normal, effortless breathing
How to count respirations without alerting the patient

read.plain:
Before you can spot breathing that is wrong, you need a clear picture of breathing that is right. Normal breathing has three parts: rate, depth, and effort. All three have to be in range.

Rate is breaths per minute, and it depends on age. An adult breathes 12 to 20 times a minute. A child, roughly age one through twelve, breathes faster, about 15 to 30. An infant under a year breathes faster still, about 25 to 50. Memorize all three, because a rate of 28 is normal for a toddler and worrying for an adult.

Depth is how much air moves with each breath. You judge it by looking: the chest should rise visibly and evenly on both sides. Put a hand on the chest if you need to. Shallow breathing with barely any chest movement is a warning sign even if the rate is fine.

Effort is how hard the patient is working. Normal breathing is quiet and looks easy. The neck and shoulder muscles are not straining, the skin between the ribs is not sucking in, the nostrils are not flaring, and the person can talk in full sentences without stopping for air. Any of those signs means breathing is no longer effortless.

Count the rate by watching the chest for 30 seconds and doubling it. A trick: keep your fingers on the wrist as if you are still taking a pulse. If a patient knows you are counting their breaths, the number changes.
read.standard:
Normal respiratory rates vary with age. Adults breathe at approximately 12 to 20 breaths per minute, children (1 to 12 years) at approximately 15 to 30, and infants (under 1 year) at approximately 25 to 50. Rates above or below these ranges in a symptomatic patient warrant further assessment, but rate must be interpreted alongside depth and effort.

Adequate depth is assessed by observing symmetric chest rise; tidal volume cannot be measured in the field but is inferred from visible excursion and, when auscultated, breath sounds present in all fields. Normal breathing is quiet, regular, and effortless, without accessory muscle use of the sternocleidomastoid or intercostal muscles, without supraclavicular, intercostal, or subcostal retractions, and without nasal flaring or tripod positioning. A patient breathing normally can speak full sentences without pausing.

Respirations are counted over 30 seconds and doubled, ideally while the EMT appears to still be palpating a radial pulse, because conscious awareness alters respiratory pattern. Rhythm should be regular; irregular patterns, periods of apnea, or agonal gasps indicate inadequate breathing regardless of the counted rate.

eli_new.analogy: Normal breathing is like a good idle on a car engine: steady, quiet, not revving, not stalling.
eli_new.body:
You check three gauges. RPM is the rate, and the normal idle depends on the model: adults 12 to 20, kids 15 to 30, infants 25 to 50. Throttle depth is how much air each breath moves; the chest should visibly rise. And the engine should sound smooth: no straining, no whistling, no knocking. If the driver can carry on a conversation without gasping, the engine is idling fine.

And do not tell the driver you are listening to the engine. People rev when they know you are watching.

story.title: Twenty-eight
story.dispatch: Rescue 6, 2-year-old female, fever and cough, daycare center.
story.body:
She is sitting in a staff member's lap, flushed, a little cranky, and clearly annoyed at you. You count while pretending to look at her wrist: 28 breaths a minute. The daycare worker sees the number on your notepad and panics. 'That's so fast.'

It is not, for her. Two-year-olds sit in the 15 to 30 range, and she is inside it. More importantly, you look at the rest: her chest rises evenly, the breathing is quiet, no flaring at the nostrils, no skin sucking in between the ribs, and she just yelled 'NO' at you in a full, loud voice. The rate is one gauge. The rest of the picture says a sick toddler who is breathing fine. You explain that to the worker while you finish the assessment, and the panic goes out of the room.

concepts.title: Adequate vs. inadequate breathing
key_points: Adequate breathing: rate in the normal range for age, regular rhythm, visible equal chest rise, quiet, effortless, patient alert and able to speak full sentences
Inadequate breathing: rate too slow or too fast for age, shallow depth, irregular rhythm, or visible effort
Signs of effort: accessory muscle use (neck and shoulder muscles), retractions (skin pulling in between or under the ribs), nasal flaring, tripod position, pursed-lip breathing
Two- or three-word dyspnea (can only speak a few words per breath) is a red flag
Late signs: cyanosis, altered mental status, agonal gasps
The decision that follows: adequate breathing with hypoxia gets supplemental oxygen; inadequate breathing gets ventilation with a BVM, not just a mask
Agonal gasps are not breathing; treat the patient as not breathing
Reassess constantly; adequate can become inadequate within minutes
misconceptions: Putting a non-rebreather on a patient whose breathing is inadequate and expecting it to help
Counting agonal gasps as respirations
Assuming a talking patient is fine without noticing they are speaking two words at a time
Waiting for cyanosis before acting (it is a late sign)
exam_favorites: The signs of inadequate breathing
Adequate breathing plus hypoxia = oxygen; inadequate breathing = BVM
Agonal gasps are not effective breathing
Cyanosis and altered mental status as late signs

read.plain:
This is the decision that the whole airway module builds toward. Every breathing patient you meet falls on one side of a line: adequate or inadequate. Which side decides what you do next.

Adequate breathing looks like normal breathing. The rate is in range for the patient's age, the rhythm is regular, the chest rises visibly and evenly, it is quiet, it looks easy, and the patient is alert and can talk in full sentences. If any of that is off, you are looking at inadequate breathing.

Inadequate breathing shows up in the rate (too fast or too slow for age), the depth (shallow, barely any chest movement), the rhythm (irregular, with pauses), or the effort. Effort is where you will catch most of them. Watch for neck and shoulder muscles pulling with each breath, skin sucking in between the ribs or below them, nostrils flaring, a patient leaning forward on their hands in the tripod position, or breathing out through pursed lips. Listen to how they talk: a patient who can only get two or three words out before gasping for air is in trouble.

The late signs are the ones you never want to be the first to notice: blue or gray skin, confusion or sleepiness, and agonal gasps. Agonal gasps are slow, irregular, snoring or gasping breaths from a brain that is shutting down. They are not breathing. A patient with agonal gasps is treated as a patient who is not breathing at all.

Now the decision. A patient whose breathing is adequate but whose oxygen level is low gets supplemental oxygen: a cannula or a non-rebreather. A patient whose breathing is inadequate gets ventilated. That means a bag-valve-mask, breathing for them or with them, because no mask sitting on the face can fix a rate or a depth that is too low. This single distinction, oxygen versus ventilation, is the most important thing in this lesson.

And it can change. A patient who was adequate five minutes ago can tire out and become inadequate. Reassess every few minutes.
read.standard:
Assessment of breathing adequacy integrates rate, rhythm, depth (tidal volume), and work of breathing against age-appropriate norms, together with mental status and the patient's ability to speak. Adequate breathing is characterized by a normal rate for age, regular rhythm, symmetric and visible chest excursion, quiet respirations without adventitious sounds audible without a stethoscope, absence of accessory muscle use, and an alert patient able to speak in full sentences.

Inadequate breathing may be evidenced by bradypnea or tachypnea for age, shallow or irregular respirations, or increased work of breathing: use of sternocleidomastoid and intercostal muscles, supraclavicular, intercostal, or subcostal retractions, nasal flaring, tripod positioning, and pursed-lip exhalation. Two- to three-word dyspnea, inability to lie flat, and audible wheezing, stridor, or gurgling are additional indicators. Cyanosis, altered mental status, and agonal respirations are late findings signifying impending respiratory failure or arrest. Agonal gasps are ineffective and are managed as apnea.

Management follows directly from the assessment. Patients with adequate breathing who are hypoxic or at risk receive supplemental oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 94% to 99%. Patients with inadequate breathing require assisted or complete positive-pressure ventilation with a bag-valve-mask and supplemental oxygen, because passive delivery devices cannot correct insufficient rate or tidal volume. Reassessment at frequent intervals is essential because adequacy can deteriorate rapidly with fatigue.

eli_new.analogy: Adequate breathing is a swimmer doing laps. Inadequate breathing is a swimmer starting to thrash.
eli_new.body:
A good swimmer looks smooth: steady strokes, regular breathing, no wasted motion. The moment they start to struggle you see it before they go under: the strokes get choppy, the head bobs, the neck strains, they cannot answer you between breaths. That is accessory muscles, retractions, and two-word sentences.

When the swimmer is only thrashing a little, you throw them a flotation ring: that is oxygen. When they are going under, a ring does nothing. You get in the water and swim for them: that is the bag-valve-mask. The whole skill is knowing which swimmer you are looking at, and looking again every couple of minutes because tired swimmers go under fast.

teach.model_answer: Inadequate breathing shows up as a rate that is too fast or too slow for age, shallow chest movement, an irregular rhythm, or visible effort: neck muscles straining, retractions, nasal flaring, tripod position, pursed lips. Patients who can only say two or three words per breath, who are confused or drowsy, or who are turning blue are in serious trouble, and agonal gasps mean they are effectively not breathing. When breathing is inadequate, oxygen alone is not enough; you ventilate with a bag-valve-mask.

story.title: The line
story.dispatch: Engine 1, Rescue 1, 66-year-old female, difficulty breathing, history of COPD, husband on scene.
story.body:
She is on the edge of the bed, hands on her knees, shoulders hunched up around her ears, breathing through pursed lips. You ask her name. 'Carol.' You ask what happened. 'Can't... breathe... since... lunch.' Three words at a time. Skin between her ribs pulls in with every breath. Rate 32. Sats 84%.

You put a non-rebreather on her at 15 and get her onto the stretcher. Two minutes later something changes. Her eyes are drifting closed. Her shoulders have stopped hunching, not because she is better but because she is too tired to fight anymore. The breaths are slower now, 8 a minute, and shallow. The bag on the mask barely moves.

She just crossed the line. The mask comes off and the BVM comes out, and you squeeze in time with her failing breaths, assisting every one. This is the whole lesson in one call: the same patient, adequate then inadequate, and the treatment changed the moment she did. If you had not reassessed, you would have missed it.

rows.right: Too fast or too slow for age
Two or three words at a time

concepts.title: Head-tilt/chin-lift
key_points: The default manual airway maneuver when nothing about the mechanism suggests a spinal injury
In an unresponsive patient the tongue is the most common cause of airway obstruction
One hand on the forehead tilts the head back; the fingers of the other hand lift the bony part of the chin
Lift the chin with fingertips on bone, not on the soft tissue under the jaw
Contraindicated when the mechanism raises suspicion of spinal injury; use the jaw-thrust instead
misconceptions: Pressing on the soft tissue under the chin, which pushes the tongue back into the airway
Using it on a trauma patient whose mechanism suggests a spinal injury
Believing the tilt itself opens the airway; it is the jaw and tongue moving forward that does
exam_favorites: When head-tilt/chin-lift is contraindicated
What actually obstructs the airway in an unresponsive patient
Choosing between head-tilt/chin-lift and jaw-thrust from the mechanism

read.plain:
When somebody is unresponsive, the muscles that normally hold the tongue forward go slack. The tongue falls back against the throat and blocks the airway. It is the single most common cause of a blocked airway in an unconscious patient, and it is the easiest one to fix.

Put one hand flat on the forehead and tilt the head back. With the fingertips of your other hand, lift the bony part of the chin upward. Keep your fingers on bone. If you press into the soft tissue under the jaw you will push the tongue backward and make things worse.

What you are really doing is moving the jaw forward. The tongue is anchored to the jaw, so when the jaw comes forward the tongue comes with it and lifts off the back of the throat. The tilt just helps line everything up.

Use this one whenever there is no reason to worry about the spine. If the patient fell, was in a crash, was struck, or you simply do not know what happened, use the jaw-thrust instead.
read.standard: The head-tilt/chin-lift is the standard manual maneuver for opening the airway of an unresponsive patient in whom spinal injury is not suspected. The operator places one hand on the patient's forehead and applies gentle posterior pressure while the fingertips of the opposite hand lift the mandible at the bony prominence of the chin. Displacement of the mandible anteriorly carries the tongue, which is attached to it, away from the posterior pharyngeal wall. Pressure on the submandibular soft tissue must be avoided, as it can displace the tongue posteriorly and worsen obstruction. The maneuver is contraindicated where the mechanism of injury suggests cervical spine involvement; in those patients the modified jaw-thrust is used.

eli_new.analogy: The tongue is a door on a hinge, and the hinge is the jaw. Move the jaw forward and the door swings open.
eli_new.body: Nobody swallows their tongue. What actually happens is simpler: the tongue is a muscle attached to the jaw, and when somebody goes unconscious everything relaxes. The tongue sags backward and rests against the back of the throat like a flap over a drain. Lift the jaw and you lift the tongue with it, because they are connected. That is all this maneuver is.

teach.prompt: Explain to a brand-new EMT what actually blocks the airway in an unresponsive patient, and how you open it when there is no reason to suspect a spinal injury.

must_hit.point: The tongue is the obstruction
Hand on the forehead, fingers lifting the bony chin
Avoid pressing the soft tissue under the jaw
Not used when spinal injury is suspected

teach.model_answer: In an unresponsive patient the tongue relaxes back against the throat and blocks the airway. Put one hand on the forehead and tilt the head back, then lift the bony part of the chin with the fingertips of your other hand. Keep off the soft tissue under the jaw, because pressing there pushes the tongue backward. Because the tongue is attached to the jaw, moving the jaw forward pulls the tongue clear. Use this only when the mechanism gives you no reason to suspect a spinal injury; if it does, use the jaw-thrust.

story.title: The snoring man
story.dispatch: Rescue 2, unresponsive male, possible overdose, apartment building.
story.body:
He is on the bathroom floor, breathing but snoring loudly with every breath. Nothing in the scene suggests a fall or a blow to the head. Your partner kneels at his head, puts a hand on his forehead, lifts the bony chin, and the snoring stops mid-breath. The chest still rises, but now it is quiet.

That sound was air forcing its way past a tongue lying against the back of his throat. Nothing was in his mouth. Nothing was swallowed. The fix took two seconds and no equipment.

concepts.title: Jaw-thrust: when and why
key_points: The airway maneuver for a patient in whom spinal injury is suspected
Opens the airway by moving the mandible forward without tilting the head
Performed from the head of the patient, fingers behind the angles of the jaw, pushing the jaw forward
Harder to hold and more tiring than a head-tilt/chin-lift, and usually needs a second rescuer for the BVM
An open airway takes priority: if the jaw-thrust does not open it, the airway still has to be opened
misconceptions: Tilting the head 'just a little' while doing it, which defeats the purpose
Choosing the maneuver from how the patient looks rather than from the mechanism of injury
Abandoning airway management because the jaw-thrust is awkward
exam_favorites: The mechanism decides the maneuver
That the jaw-thrust avoids head movement
That an open airway outranks a perfectly neutral spine

read.plain:
Sometimes you need the airway open but you do not want to move the neck. Somebody fell, or was hit, or you simply do not know what happened. The jaw-thrust gets the job done without tilting the head.

Kneel at the top of the patient's head, facing down their body. Put your fingers behind the angles of the jaw, on both sides, just below the ears. Push the jaw forward, toward the ceiling. Your thumbs can rest on the cheekbones or open the mouth slightly. The head stays exactly where it is.

It is the same idea as the chin-lift: bring the jaw forward and the tongue comes with it. You are just getting there without moving the neck.

Be honest about the trade-off. The jaw-thrust is tiring, it is awkward, and it ties up your hands, so somebody else usually has to squeeze the bag. And if you truly cannot open the airway any other way, an open airway wins. A patient with a perfect spine and no air is still dead.
read.standard: The modified jaw-thrust is the manual airway maneuver indicated when cervical spine injury is suspected. The rescuer positions at the patient's head, places the fingers behind the angles of the mandible bilaterally, and displaces the mandible anteriorly without extending the cervical spine. The thumbs may be used to retract the lower lip and open the mouth. Anterior displacement of the mandible carries the tongue off the posterior pharynx, achieving the same result as the chin-lift without cervical movement. The maneuver is more fatiguing than the head-tilt/chin-lift and generally occupies one rescuer entirely, requiring a second provider for bag-valve-mask ventilation. Airway patency remains the overriding priority.

eli_new.analogy: Same door, same hinge. You are opening it from the other side of the room so you do not have to move the wall.
eli_new.body: Think of the head-tilt/chin-lift and the jaw-thrust as two ways to do the same thing: pull the jaw forward so the tongue comes off the back of the throat. One does it by tilting, one does it by pushing from behind the jaw. When you cannot afford to tilt, you push instead.

teach.prompt: Tell a new partner when they should use a jaw-thrust instead of a head-tilt/chin-lift, and how they do it.

must_hit.point: Used when spinal injury is suspected
Fingers behind the angles of the jaw, pushing it forward

teach.model_answer: Use it whenever the mechanism makes a spinal injury plausible: a fall, a crash, a blow, or an unknown cause. Kneel at the top of the head, put your fingers behind the angles of the jaw on both sides, and push the jaw forward toward the ceiling without tilting the head. The tongue is attached to the jaw, so bringing the jaw forward lifts the tongue off the back of the throat. It is tiring and it uses both your hands, so somebody else works the bag.

story.title: Down the stairs
story.dispatch: Rescue 2, Engine 4 — fall from height, basement stairs, patient not moving.
story.body:
He is at the foot of the stairs, unresponsive, breathing shallowly. Your partner holds the head still while you kneel above it. Fingers behind the angles of the jaw, push forward. The breathing gets quieter and deeper.

You hold that for eleven minutes, which is a long time when your forearms are burning, while your partner bags and the medic sets up. You do not tilt. You do not adjust. You just hold the jaw where the air moves.

rows.left: One can manage airway and bag

concepts.title: Recovery position
key_points: For an unresponsive patient who is breathing adequately and has no suspected spinal injury
Lateral recumbent position lets fluid drain out of the mouth rather than into the airway
Not used when the mechanism suggests spinal injury, or when the patient needs ventilation
The patient still needs continuous monitoring; the position is not a substitute for reassessment
misconceptions: Placing a trauma patient in the recovery position
Using it as a reason to stop watching the airway
Using it on a patient who is not breathing adequately
exam_favorites: Which patient gets the recovery position
Why lateral, not supine
That it does not replace reassessment

read.plain:
Somebody who is unconscious but breathing fine has one main enemy: their own stomach contents. Lying on their back, anything that comes up goes straight down. Rolled onto their side, it runs out of the mouth and onto the floor, which is exactly where you want it.

Roll the patient as a unit onto their side, so the head, shoulders and hips move together. The mouth ends up as the lowest point of the face. Support the head so the airway stays in line.

Two rules limit it. If the mechanism suggests a spinal injury, do not roll them for position alone. And if the patient is not breathing adequately, position is not the problem you are solving; they need ventilation.

The position buys you drainage, not safety. Stay at the head and keep reassessing.
read.standard: The recovery position is a lateral recumbent position used for the unresponsive patient with adequate spontaneous ventilation and no suspected spinal injury. Placing the patient laterally allows secretions, blood and vomit to drain from the mouth by gravity rather than pooling in the posterior pharynx, reducing aspiration risk. The patient is rolled as a unit to maintain spinal alignment, with the head supported so that the airway remains patent and the mouth dependent. The position is contraindicated where spinal injury is suspected and is not a substitute for ventilation in a patient with inadequate breathing. Continuous airway monitoring and reassessment are required regardless of position.

eli_new.analogy: Tip the cup so it drains onto the floor instead of filling up.
eli_new.body: Your patient is a cup with liquid in it. Face up, anything that comes up sits in the cup and eventually goes down the wrong pipe. Turn the cup on its side and the same liquid runs out harmlessly. That is the whole idea.

teach.prompt: Explain which unresponsive patients get put in the recovery position and which do not, and why the position helps.

must_hit.point: Unresponsive but breathing adequately
No suspected spinal injury
Lets fluid drain out of the mouth

teach.model_answer: An unresponsive patient who is breathing adequately and has no mechanism suggesting spinal injury goes on their side. Rolled as a unit, with the mouth as the lowest point, anything that comes up drains out instead of down. A patient whose mechanism suggests a spinal injury does not get rolled for position alone, and a patient who is not breathing adequately needs ventilation rather than repositioning. Either way you stay at the head and keep reassessing.

story.title: After the seizure
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 24-year-old female, seizure, now postictal, private residence.
story.body:
The seizure stopped before you arrived. She is unresponsive but breathing deeply and evenly, and there is saliva pooling at the corner of her mouth. Her mother says she slid off the sofa onto the carpet, nothing else.

You roll her onto her side as a unit and support her head. Within a few seconds a thin string of saliva runs out onto the towel you put down instead of sitting at the back of her throat. You stay at her head with the suction ready and watch her breathe.

concepts.title: Oropharyngeal airway: sizing, insertion, contraindication
key_points: Holds the tongue off the back of the throat in a patient with no gag reflex
Sized from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or to the angle of the jaw
Contraindicated in any patient with an intact gag reflex
In an adult, inserted with the tip toward the roof of the mouth and rotated 180 degrees as it passes the soft palate
In a child, inserted right side up with a tongue depressor rather than rotated
Too long presses on the epiglottis; too short leaves the tongue obstructing
An airway adjunct does not replace a manual maneuver; keep the head positioned
misconceptions: Inserting an OPA in a patient who still has a gag reflex
Using the rotation technique in a small child
Believing the adjunct means the manual maneuver can be released
Guessing the size instead of measuring against the patient's face
exam_favorites: The measurement landmarks
The gag reflex contraindication
The 180-degree rotation in adults and why children differ
What happens if it is too long or too short

read.plain:
An oropharyngeal airway is a curved piece of plastic that sits over the tongue and holds it off the back of the throat. It does mechanically what your chin-lift does with your hands, so you can let go and do something else.

It only works in a patient who is deeply unconscious. If there is any gag reflex, the OPA will trigger vomiting, and now you have a bigger problem than the one you started with. No gag, no problem; any gag, use something else.

Size it against the patient's own face: hold it from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or to the angle of the jaw. Too long and the tip presses the epiglottis down over the opening. Too short and the tongue is still in the way.

In an adult, open the mouth, put the tip in pointing at the roof of the mouth, slide it in, and rotate it 180 degrees as it passes the soft palate so it settles into position. In a child, do not rotate it. Hold the tongue down with a tongue depressor and slide it in the right way up, because a child's palate is easily damaged.

One last thing. The adjunct holds the tongue, not the head. Keep the head positioned.
read.standard: The oropharyngeal airway (OPA) is a rigid curved adjunct that maintains patency by holding the tongue away from the posterior pharyngeal wall. It is indicated only in patients without a gag reflex, and an intact gag reflex is an absolute contraindication owing to the risk of vomiting and aspiration. Sizing is performed against the patient by measuring from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or to the angle of the mandible. An oversized device may displace the epiglottis and occlude the glottic opening; an undersized device fails to control the tongue. In adults the device is conventionally introduced with the tip directed toward the hard palate and rotated 180 degrees as it passes the soft palate. In pediatric patients rotation is avoided because of the risk of soft-tissue and palatal trauma; the tongue is displaced with a tongue blade and the device inserted in its anatomic orientation. Insertion of an adjunct does not obviate the need for continued manual airway positioning.

eli_new.analogy: It is a shoehorn for the tongue: it holds the thing that keeps collapsing out of the way so your hands are free.
eli_new.body: Your chin-lift works, but you cannot hold it forever and you have other jobs. The OPA is a piece of plastic shaped to do the holding for you. The catch is that it sits deep enough to make an awake person gag and vomit, so it is only for patients who are far enough under that they do not react at all.

teach.prompt: Walk a new EMT through sizing and inserting an oropharyngeal airway in an adult, and tell them the one patient who must never get one.

teach.model_answer: Measure it against the patient's own face, from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or the angle of the jaw. Check for a gag reflex first: if there is any gag at all, an OPA is out. In an adult, open the mouth, insert the tip pointing up at the roof of the mouth, slide it in and rotate it 180 degrees as it passes the soft palate so it seats over the tongue. In a child you do not rotate it; you hold the tongue down with a tongue depressor and slide it in the right way up. Too long presses on the epiglottis, too short leaves the tongue in the way, and either way you still keep the head positioned.

story.title: Measured against the wrong face
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — unresponsive male, found by coworkers, warehouse floor.
story.body:
He is deeply unconscious and has no gag at all. Your partner pulls an OPA off the tray by eye, and it is obviously the one from the top of the box rather than the one that fits this man.

You hold it against his cheek: corner of the mouth to the earlobe. It is two sizes too long. You swap it, insert the right one with a rotation, and the breathing you are supporting gets easier straight away. The wrong one would have pushed the epiglottis down over the very opening you were trying to protect.

read.plain:
The nasopharyngeal airway is a soft rubber tube that goes in through the nose and sits behind the tongue. Its advantage over the OPA is simple: most patients tolerate it even with a gag reflex, so you can use it on somebody who is not deeply unconscious.

Size the length against the patient, from the tip of the nose to the earlobe. Lubricate it with a water-soluble lubricant, never petroleum.

Now the part people get wrong. The floor of the nasal cavity runs straight back, not up. Point the tip straight toward the back of the head, with the bevel facing the septum, and advance gently. If you aim it up toward the bridge of the nose it will not go, and you will make it bleed.

There is one situation to avoid. If the face or head is badly injured and you are worried about a skull fracture, do not put a tube into the nose.

And be clear about what it does not do. It holds the tongue off the throat. It does not keep vomit out of the lungs. Suction stays within reach.
read.standard: The nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) is a soft, uncuffed adjunct inserted through the nares into the posterior pharynx. Unlike the oropharyngeal airway it is generally tolerated in patients with an intact gag reflex, making it suitable for the obtunded patient who will not accept an OPA. Length is estimated externally by measuring from the tip of the nose to the earlobe. The device is lubricated with a water-soluble lubricant and advanced posteriorly along the floor of the nasal cavity with the bevel oriented toward the nasal septum; the nasal floor runs directly posteriorly, and superior angulation causes trauma and failure of passage. The NPA is avoided in the presence of significant head or mid-facial trauma where basilar skull fracture is suspected. The adjunct maintains patency but confers no protection against regurgitation or aspiration, and suction must remain immediately available.

eli_new.analogy: The nose is a hallway, not a staircase. Walk straight down it; do not try to climb.
eli_new.body: Everyone's instinct is to aim a tube up into the nose, because that is the direction the nose points on the outside. Inside, the passage runs flat, straight toward the back of the skull. Aim straight back and it slides. Aim up and you hit bone and cause a nosebleed.

Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe for length, lubricate it with a water-soluble lubricant, and insert it with the bevel toward the septum, advancing straight back along the floor of the nose rather than up toward the bridge. Avoid it where significant head or mid-face trauma makes a skull fracture plausible. Remember it holds the tongue forward but does nothing to stop vomit, so keep suction to hand.

He is snoring, will not stay awake, and gags hard when your partner even approaches his mouth with a suction tip. An OPA is out.

You size an NPA against his face, nose to earlobe, lubricate it, and start it straight back along the floor of the nostril with the bevel turned toward the septum. It passes without a fight. The snoring stops. He does not gag once.

The new EMT riding with you had it angled upward on the first attempt and could not understand why it would not go.

read.plain:
Positioning fixes a tongue. It does nothing about blood, vomit or secretions. For those you need suction.

There are two tips. The rigid one, sometimes called a tonsil tip or Yankauer, is for the mouth, and it is the one for thick material. The soft flexible catheter is for the nose, a stoma, or for going through an airway adjunct; it is narrow and clogs on anything chunky.

Measure before you insert, the same way you size an OPA: corner of the mouth to the earlobe. That is as deep as the tip goes.

Here is the part that matters most. Put the tip in with the suction off. Only turn it on as you pull back out, sweeping as you go. Suction on the way in grabs the tissue you are sliding past and does no good at all.

And remember what you are removing. Suction takes out air along with the fluid, so you cannot just keep going. Work in limited passes, then put oxygen or ventilation back on, then go again if you need to.

If the patient vomits, everything stops. Roll them, clear it out, and only then go back to what you were doing.
read.standard: Suctioning removes liquid and semi-solid material from the airway that positioning and adjuncts cannot clear. Rigid pharyngeal (tonsil-tip) catheters are used for the oropharynx and for thick material; soft flexible catheters are used for the nasopharynx, tracheostomy stomas, and passage through an airway adjunct. Insertion depth is estimated externally using the same landmarks as OPA sizing, from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, and the catheter should not be advanced beyond the measured depth. Suction is applied only during withdrawal, using a sweeping motion; applying suction during insertion causes mucosal trauma without clearing material. Because suctioning evacuates oxygen along with secretions, it is performed in limited passes with reoxygenation or ventilation between attempts. Active vomiting takes precedence over all other airway interventions: the patient is positioned to allow drainage and the airway cleared before ventilation resumes.

eli_new.analogy: A straw in a milkshake. You push the straw in quietly, and you only start sucking on the way back out.
eli_new.body: Nobody suctions on the way in, and there is a reason. Going in, the tip is sliding past soft tissue. If the vacuum is already on, it grabs that tissue, hurts the patient, and clears nothing, because the mess you want is behind it. Go in quiet, come out sucking.

teach.prompt: Explain to a new EMT which suction tip to grab, how far to put it in, and the one rule about when the suction is actually switched on.

must_hit.point: Rigid tip for the mouth and thick material, soft catheter for nose, stoma or adjunct
Measure corner of the mouth to the earlobe
Suction only on the way out
Limited passes, because suction removes oxygen too

teach.model_answer: Use the rigid tonsil tip in the mouth, especially for thick material, and the soft flexible catheter for the nose, a stoma, or through an adjunct. Measure the depth against the face just like an OPA, corner of the mouth to the earlobe, and do not go past it. Put the tip in with the suction off and only switch it on as you withdraw, sweeping as you come out. Keep each pass short, because you are pulling out oxygen along with the fluid, and reoxygenate or ventilate between passes. If the patient is actively vomiting, roll them and clear it before anything else.

story.title: The sound before the vomit
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — unresponsive female, possible stroke, found by husband.
story.body:
You are two breaths into bagging her when you hear it: a wet, gurgling catch at the back of the throat. Your partner already has the rigid tip in hand, measured against her cheek.

You stop bagging. Roll her. In with the suction off, on as it comes out, one sweep. Then back onto her back, reposition, and ventilate again. A few seconds later the same sound starts, and you do it again.

Bagging through that gurgle would have pushed all of it down into her lungs.

concepts.title: Foreign body airway obstruction management by age
key_points: A mild obstruction with good air exchange is left alone to cough; interfering can make it complete
A severe obstruction cannot speak, cough effectively, or move air, and needs immediate intervention
A responsive adult or child over one year gets abdominal thrusts
A responsive infant under one year gets alternating back slaps and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts
Chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts in late pregnancy or a patient too large to encircle
When the patient becomes unresponsive, begin CPR and look in the mouth each time you open the airway
Remove an object only if you can see it; blind finger sweeps are not performed
misconceptions: Intervening on a patient who is still coughing forcefully
Using abdominal thrusts on an infant
Performing a blind finger sweep
Stopping compressions to keep trying thrusts after the patient goes unresponsive
exam_favorites: Mild versus severe and what each gets
The age cut-off at one year
Chest thrusts in pregnancy or obesity
No blind finger sweeps
What changes the moment the patient becomes unresponsive

read.plain:
The first decision is not what to do; it is how bad it is. A patient who is coughing hard, wheezing between coughs and moving air has a mild obstruction, and the best thing you can do is stand there and encourage them. Their cough generates more pressure than your hands will.

A severe obstruction looks different. No sound, or a thin high-pitched squeak. Cannot speak. Cannot cough. Maybe clutching the throat. That patient needs you now.

For a responsive adult or a child over one year, abdominal thrusts. Stand behind, fist above the navel and below the ribs, and thrust inward and upward, repeating until it clears or they go unresponsive.

An infant under one year is different. Support the head and jaw, face down along your forearm, and deliver back slaps between the shoulder blades, then turn them over and give chest thrusts. Alternate. No abdominal thrusts in an infant.

If the patient is in late pregnancy or you simply cannot get your arms around them, move your hands to the chest and thrust there instead.

The moment they go unresponsive, everything changes. Lower them to the floor and start CPR. Every time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth first. If you see the object, take it out. If you do not see it, do not go fishing.
read.standard: Foreign body airway obstruction is classified by the adequacy of air exchange. Mild obstruction, characterized by forceful coughing and audible air movement, is managed by encouraging the patient to continue coughing; intervention risks converting a partial obstruction to a complete one. Severe obstruction is recognized by the inability to speak, cough effectively, or move air, and may be accompanied by high-pitched stridor or the universal choking sign. In the responsive adult or child older than one year, abdominal thrusts are delivered above the umbilicus and below the xiphoid process, directed inward and upward, and repeated until the obstruction is relieved or the patient becomes unresponsive. In the infant under one year, abdominal thrusts are not used; management consists of alternating back slaps delivered between the scapulae with the infant supported prone and head-dependent, and chest thrusts delivered supine. Chest thrusts substitute for abdominal thrusts in late pregnancy or where the rescuer cannot encircle the abdomen. When the patient becomes unresponsive, chest compressions are initiated; the mouth is inspected each time the airway is opened for ventilation and a visualized object removed. Blind finger sweeps are not performed.

eli_new.analogy: A cough is a bigger, better-aimed thrust than anything you can do with your hands. Do not interrupt a working cough.
eli_new.body: Two questions, in order. Can they move air? If yes, leave them alone and let them cough. If no, you act. Then: how old are they? Over one, thrusts to the belly. Under one, slaps to the back and thrusts to the chest. That is the whole algorithm.

teach.prompt: Explain how you decide whether to intervene in a choking patient at all, and how what you do changes with the patient's age.

must_hit.point: Mild obstruction with a forceful cough is left to cough
Severe means cannot speak, cough or move air

teach.model_answer: First decide how bad it is. If they are coughing forcefully and moving air, that is a mild obstruction and your job is to encourage the cough and stay ready. If they cannot speak, cannot cough and are not moving air, that is severe and you act immediately. For a responsive adult or a child over one, abdominal thrusts above the navel and below the ribs, inward and upward, until it clears or they go out. For an infant under one, no abdominal thrusts: support them face down along your forearm for back slaps between the shoulder blades, then turn them for chest thrusts, and alternate. Use chest thrusts instead on a patient in late pregnancy or one you cannot get your arms around. If they become unresponsive, lower them down and start CPR, and each time you open the airway to ventilate, look in the mouth and remove anything you can actually see. Never sweep blindly.

story.title: The quiet table
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — choking, restaurant, bystander CPR in progress.
story.body:
The room is loud but the table you are walking toward is silent. A man is standing with both hands at his throat and a waiter behind him is delivering thrusts. He is not making any sound at all.

On the fourth thrust after you arrive, something gives and he takes a huge ragged breath. Within a minute he is talking, embarrassed, insisting he is fine.

What stays with you is the silence. Everyone expects choking to be noisy. The dangerous ones are not.

concepts.title: Oxygen cylinders, regulators, and safety
key_points: Oxygen is stored as a compressed gas in green (US) steel or aluminum cylinders
Common EMS sizes: D (about 350 L) and E (about 625 L) portable; M (about 3,000 L) onboard the ambulance
A full cylinder reads about 2,000 psi; replace or refill at the safe residual pressure of 200 psi
A regulator reduces cylinder pressure to a safe working pressure and a flowmeter sets liters per minute
Duration (min) = (gauge psi − 200) × cylinder constant ÷ flow rate in L/min
Cylinder constants: D = 0.16, E = 0.28, M = 1.56
Never use oil, grease, or petroleum products near oxygen equipment; keep cylinders secured and away from heat and open flame
Cylinders must be hydrostatically tested on a schedule (every 5 years for most; the date is stamped on the cylinder)
misconceptions: Thinking oxygen itself is flammable (it is not, but it makes other things burn faster and hotter)
Running a cylinder to 0 psi instead of swapping at 200 psi
Forgetting to subtract the safe residual pressure in the duration calculation
Laying an unsecured cylinder loose in the ambulance
exam_favorites: The safe residual pressure (200 psi)
Duration of flow calculation with a D or E cylinder
Safety rules: no petroleum products, secure the cylinder, keep away from heat

read.plain:
Every breath of oxygen you give a patient starts in a green metal tank. Oxygen is squeezed into the cylinder as a gas at very high pressure, about 2,000 psi when full. That pressure is far too high to send to a patient, so a regulator screws onto the cylinder and steps it down to a safe working pressure. A flowmeter on the regulator lets you dial in how many liters per minute the patient gets.

You will use two portable sizes constantly: the D cylinder (roughly 350 liters) that rides in your jump bag, and the E cylinder (roughly 625 liters) that fits on the stretcher. The big M cylinder (roughly 3,000 liters) lives in the ambulance and feeds the wall outlets.

The gauge tells you how much is left. When it reads 200 psi, that is your safe residual pressure: swap the tank. Below that, the flow becomes unreliable and moisture or contaminants can get in. Never plan to run a tank dry.

Safety matters because oxygen feeds fire. It is not flammable on its own, but anything burning in oxygen-rich air burns fast and hot. So: no smoking, no open flame, no oil or grease on any fitting, and always keep the cylinder secured so it cannot fall or roll. A knocked-over cylinder with the valve sheared off becomes a rocket.
read.standard:
Oxygen cylinders are color-coded green in the United States and labeled with the contents. Sizes used in EMS include D (about 350 L), E (about 625 L), and M (about 3,000 L). A full cylinder is pressurized to approximately 2,000 psi. A pressure regulator reduces this to a working pressure (typically 40 to 70 psi), and a flowmeter, either a pressure-compensated or a Bourdon-gauge type, controls the flow in liters per minute. The pin-index safety system ensures a regulator can only be attached to the correct gas.

To calculate how long a cylinder will last: Duration (minutes) = (gauge pressure in psi − 200 psi safe residual) × cylinder constant ÷ flow rate (L/min). Constants: D = 0.16, E = 0.28, M = 1.56. Example: an E cylinder at 2,000 psi running at 15 L/min lasts (2,000 − 200) × 0.28 ÷ 15 = 33.6 minutes.

Safety: keep cylinders secured in transport, store away from heat and combustibles, never use petroleum-based lubricants, open the valve slowly, and stand to the side of the regulator when opening. Cylinders require hydrostatic testing on a fixed schedule; the last test date is stamped on the cylinder.

eli_new.analogy: A cylinder is a scuba tank for your patient, and the regulator is the mouthpiece that makes the pressure survivable.
eli_new.body:
Think of a fire hose hooked straight to a hydrant with no nozzle. That is 2,000 psi of oxygen with no regulator: useless and dangerous. The regulator is the nozzle that tames it. The flowmeter is the trigger you squeeze a little or a lot.

The 200 psi rule is like the gas light in your car. When it comes on you can still drive a bit, but you do not plan a road trip on it. You swap the tank.

The duration formula is just: how much is really in there (pressure minus the 200 you will not use), times how big the tank is (the constant), divided by how fast you are pouring it out (the flow rate). Bigger tank, bigger constant. Faster flow, shorter time.

do.prompt: You have an E cylinder reading 1,400 psi and a patient on a non-rebreather at 15 L/min. How many minutes of oxygen do you have?

teach.prompt: Explain to a new partner how to tell if a cylinder needs to be swapped and how to figure out how long it will last.

must_hit.point: Swap at the safe residual pressure
Duration uses the constant for the cylinder size
Divide by the flow rate

teach.model_answer: Check the gauge. At 200 psi the tank is at safe residual and gets swapped, because flow gets unreliable below that. To know how long it lasts, take the gauge pressure, subtract 200, multiply by the cylinder constant (0.16 for a D, 0.28 for an E), and divide by the flow rate in liters per minute. That gives you minutes.

story.title: The tank that was almost empty
story.dispatch: Rescue 5, respond for a 71-year-old female, shortness of breath, third-floor apartment, no elevator.
story.body:
You grab the jump bag and the D cylinder and start up the stairs. Your partner glances at the gauge on the way: 600 psi. Enough for the assessment, maybe, but this patient is going to need a non-rebreather at 15 liters, and (600 − 200) × 0.16 ÷ 15 is a little over four minutes. Your partner radios the engine crew arriving behind you to bring the E cylinder from the stretcher.

Upstairs the patient is sitting bolt upright, speaking two words at a time, sats 86%. You put her on the NRB from the D tank while the E arrives ninety seconds later. You swap the regulator over, and the D cylinder goes back on the truck tagged for refill. Nobody had to make her wait for oxygen because someone read a gauge on a staircase.

concepts.title: Nasal cannula
key_points: Two prongs that sit just inside the nostrils, tubing looped over the ears
Flow rate 1 to 6 L/min
Delivers roughly 24% to 44% oxygen
For patients who are breathing adequately and need low-concentration supplemental oxygen
Above 6 L/min the nasal passages dry out and concentration does not meaningfully rise; switch to a mask
Useless for a mouth-breather or a patient with blocked nasal passages
misconceptions: Cranking a cannula to 10 or 15 L/min expecting more oxygen
Using a cannula on a patient in obvious respiratory distress who needs a non-rebreather
Thinking the prongs go deep into the nose
exam_favorites: Flow range 1 to 6 L/min and 24 to 44% concentration
Which patient gets a cannula versus a non-rebreather

read.plain:
The nasal cannula is the gentlest way to give oxygen. Two small prongs rest just inside the nostrils, the tubing loops over the ears, and a slider snugs it under the chin. It is comfortable, it lets the patient talk and eat, and it does not feel like suffocation the way a mask can to an anxious patient.

It runs at 1 to 6 liters per minute and bumps the oxygen the patient breathes from room air (21%) up to somewhere between 24% and 44%. That is a modest boost, which is exactly the point. It is for the patient who is breathing fine on their own but whose oxygen saturation is a little low, or who has a condition where a little supplemental oxygen helps.

Do not go above 6 L/min. The nose dries out, it gets uncomfortable, and you do not gain much concentration. If the patient needs more than a cannula can give, that is a mask decision, not a flow-rate decision.

It also does nothing for a patient who breathes through their mouth, or whose nose is blocked by swelling, blood, or a deviated septum. Watch how they breathe before you pick the device.
read.standard: A nasal cannula delivers low-flow oxygen at 1 to 6 L/min, producing an inspired oxygen concentration of approximately 24% to 44% depending on flow and the patient's breathing pattern. It is indicated for patients with adequate spontaneous ventilation who require low-concentration supplemental oxygen, typically when SpO2 is mildly reduced or per protocol for specific conditions. Flow above 6 L/min causes mucosal drying and discomfort without a proportional gain in FiO2. Humidification may be added for prolonged use. Contraindications are relative: mouth breathing, nasal obstruction, and severe hypoxia that requires high-concentration delivery.

eli_new.analogy: A cannula is a garden hose trickling into a pool. A non-rebreather is the fire hose.
eli_new.body:
Room air is 21% oxygen. A cannula adds a gentle trickle on top of each breath the patient takes: 1 to 6 liters a minute, which nudges what they breathe up into the 24 to 44% range. It is a top-up, not a rescue.

Turning the trickle up past 6 does not turn it into a fire hose; it just blasts dry air up someone's nose. When a patient needs a lot of oxygen, you change the device, not the dial.

teach.prompt: Tell a new EMT when they should reach for a nasal cannula and when they should not.

must_hit.point: Adequate breathing, needs a little oxygen
1 to 6 L/min
Not for distress or mouth breathers

teach.model_answer: Use a cannula on a patient who is breathing fine on their own but has a mildly low sat or a condition that calls for a little supplemental oxygen. Run it at 1 to 6 liters per minute. Do not use it on someone in real distress who needs high-concentration oxygen, and do not use it on a mouth breather or someone with a blocked nose because the oxygen never reaches them.

story.title: Two words at a time
story.dispatch: Medic 12, 58-year-old male, chest discomfort, alert and oriented, private residence.
story.body:
He meets you at the door, talking in full sentences, a little pale, hand on his chest. Pulse ox reads 92% on room air. He is not in distress; he is worried. You sit him down and reach for the nasal cannula, set it at 2 L/min, and his sats climb to 96% within a minute while you finish your assessment and get him to the truck.

On a different call last week, a woman could only speak two words at a time and her sats were 84%. Nobody reached for a cannula that day. Same shelf in the bag, completely different device, because the question you ask first is not 'does he need oxygen?' but 'how much, and how well is he breathing on his own?'

concepts.verify_notes: Confirm flow range (1 to 6 L/min) and concentration range (24 to 44%) against AAOS 12e.

concepts.title: Non-rebreather mask
key_points: The EMT's preferred device for high-concentration oxygen in a patient who is breathing adequately
Flow rate 10 to 15 L/min; commonly set at 15
Delivers up to about 90% oxygen
Inflate the reservoir bag fully before placing the mask on the patient
One-way valves keep exhaled air out of the reservoir so the patient does not rebreathe it
The reservoir should never collapse more than about a third during inhalation; if it does, increase the flow
Requires adequate spontaneous breathing; an apneic or inadequately breathing patient needs a BVM instead
misconceptions: Putting a non-rebreather on a patient who is not breathing adequately (they need ventilation, not a mask)
Applying the mask with the reservoir bag flat
Running it below 10 L/min, which lets the bag collapse and drops the concentration
Believing the mask delivers 100% oxygen
exam_favorites: Flow rate 10 to 15 L/min and ~90% concentration
Inflating the reservoir before application
NRB versus BVM: the breathing-adequacy decision

read.plain:
When a patient needs a lot of oxygen and is still breathing on their own, the non-rebreather mask is your tool. It is a face mask with a soft bag hanging off the bottom. Oxygen flows into the bag, and each time the patient inhales they draw from that bag through a one-way valve. When they exhale, flaps on the mask open and their breath goes out into the room, not back into the bag. That is why it is called a non-rebreather.

Set the flow at 10 to 15 liters per minute. Most crews just set 15. Before the mask touches the face, put your thumb over the valve inside the mask so the bag fills completely. A full bag means the patient's first breath is oxygen-rich. Then seal the mask over the nose and mouth and tighten the strap.

Watch the bag. It should not go flat more than about a third with each breath. If it collapses, turn the flow up. At the right flow, the mask gives up to about 90% oxygen, which is the most an EMT can deliver without ventilating.

The one thing it cannot do is breathe for the patient. If the breathing is too slow, too shallow, or absent, the mask is just oxygen sitting on a face. That patient needs a bag-valve-mask.
read.standard: The non-rebreather (NRB) mask is the delivery device of choice for high-concentration oxygen in the spontaneously breathing patient with adequate tidal volume and rate. At 10 to 15 L/min it delivers an inspired oxygen concentration of up to approximately 90%. A reservoir bag is filled before application by occluding the inlet valve; the bag should remain at least two-thirds inflated during inspiration, and flow should be increased if it collapses. One-way valves prevent exhaled gas from entering the reservoir. Indications include hypoxia with adequate breathing, shock, and any condition where high FiO2 is warranted per protocol. The NRB is inappropriate for patients with inadequate ventilation, who require positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM.

eli_new.analogy: The reservoir bag is a full glass of oxygen the patient sips from; the valves make sure they never spit back into the glass.
eli_new.body:
Picture a glass being refilled from a tap at 15 liters a minute. The patient drinks from the glass (inhales), and the glass refills before the next sip. If the tap is too slow, the glass empties and they end up drinking air instead. That is why you never run it under 10, and why you fill the glass before you hand it over.

The flap valves are the 'no backwash' rule. Exhaled breath is low on oxygen and high on carbon dioxide. The valves let it out into the room instead of back into the glass. That single design detail is what pushes the concentration up to 90%.

Set the flow at 15 liters per minute, cover the valve inside the mask so the reservoir fills all the way, then seal the mask over the nose and mouth and snug the strap. Watch the bag: it should not collapse more than about a third when they breathe in. If it does, turn the flow up. Reassess their sats and work of breathing.

story.title: Fill the bag
story.dispatch: Engine 3, Rescue 3, 44-year-old male, difficulty breathing, possible asthma, convenience store.
story.body:
He is leaning on the counter with his hands on his knees, speaking in short bursts, wheezing you can hear from the door. Sats 87%. Breathing fast but moving air, chest rising well. You reach for the non-rebreather, crank the flow to 15, and hold your thumb over the inlet until the bag is round and tight. Only then does it go on his face.

Your partner is already pulling the SAMPLE history and reaching for his inhaler. Within two minutes the sats are at 93% and climbing, and the bag is filling fully between each breath. You keep watching it. If it ever starts to collapse, or if he stops being able to move air on his own, the mask comes off and the BVM comes out. Tonight it does not come to that.

Attach the mask tubing to the flowmeter and set 10 to 15 L/min
Occlude the inlet valve to fully inflate the reservoir bag before application
Place the mask over the nose and mouth and tighten the strap for a seal
Confirm the bag does not collapse more than one-third on inhalation; increase flow if it does
Reassess SpO2, work of breathing, and mental status
