concepts.title: Other delivery devices: partial rebreather, Venturi, humidified oxygen
key_points: Partial rebreather mask: looks like an NRB but has no one-way valve between mask and bag, so some exhaled air is rebreathed; delivers roughly 40% to 60% at 6 to 10 L/min; rarely used in EMS
Venturi mask: uses color-coded adapters to deliver a precise concentration (about 24% to 50%); used for patients who need a controlled, exact FiO2, classically some COPD patients
Humidified oxygen: bubbles oxygen through sterile water to reduce drying; useful on long transports and for pediatric patients; not needed for short calls
Tracheostomy mask: fits over a stoma to deliver oxygen to a patient who breathes through the neck
Awareness-level devices for the EMT; the workhorses remain the cannula, the NRB, and the BVM
misconceptions: Confusing a partial rebreather with a non-rebreather (the valve is the difference)
Thinking the Venturi mask is a high-concentration device
exam_favorites: Which device delivers a precise, controlled concentration (Venturi)
What makes a partial rebreather different from an NRB

read.plain:
You will spend almost all of your career with three devices: the cannula, the non-rebreather, and the bag-valve-mask. But a few others show up in the ambulance, in the hospital, and on the exam, and you need to recognize them.

The partial rebreather mask looks almost identical to a non-rebreather, but it is missing the one-way valve between the mask and the bag. That means a bit of each exhaled breath goes back into the bag and gets breathed again. It delivers a middling concentration, somewhere around 40 to 60%, at 6 to 10 liters per minute. It is uncommon in the field.

The Venturi mask is the precision tool. It comes with color-coded plastic adapters, and each one mixes a fixed ratio of room air with oxygen to deliver an exact percentage, roughly 24% to 50%. It is used when a doctor wants a specific concentration, most famously for certain COPD patients whose breathing is sensitive to too much oxygen.

Humidified oxygen just means the gas bubbles through sterile water before reaching the patient. Dry oxygen irritates the airway over time, so humidification helps on long transports and with kids. It is not something you set up for a ten-minute ride.

A tracheostomy mask is a small mask that sits over a stoma in the neck for patients who breathe that way.
read.standard: Partial rebreather masks lack the inspiratory one-way valve of the NRB, allowing partial rebreathing of exhaled gas; they deliver approximately 40% to 60% oxygen at 6 to 10 L/min. Venturi masks entrain room air through calibrated, color-coded jet adapters to deliver a fixed FiO2 of roughly 24% to 50%, permitting precise titration for patients with chronic CO2 retention or other conditions requiring a controlled concentration. Humidifiers add moisture to the oxygen stream to reduce mucosal drying during prolonged administration and in pediatric patients. Tracheostomy masks deliver oxygen over a stoma. These devices are awareness-level for the EMT.

eli_new.analogy: The Venturi mask is the mixing valve on a shower: you set the exact temperature and it stays there.
eli_new.body:
A non-rebreather is 'as hot as it goes.' A cannula is 'a little warm.' The Venturi mask lets you dial in the precise temperature, because each colored adapter mixes a fixed amount of room air with the oxygen. That precision is what a doctor wants for a patient whose body reacts badly to too much oxygen.

The partial rebreather is the NRB's cheaper cousin: same shape, but a valve was left out, so the patient gets a bit of their own exhaled breath back. Less oxygen, less precise, less used.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between a partial rebreather, a non-rebreather, and a Venturi mask in your own words.

must_hit.point: Partial rebreather lacks the one-way valve
Venturi delivers a precise concentration

teach.model_answer: A non-rebreather has one-way valves so the patient only gets fresh oxygen from the bag, which is why it reaches about 90%. A partial rebreather looks the same but is missing that valve, so some exhaled air gets rebreathed and the concentration is lower. A Venturi mask uses color-coded adapters to mix a set amount of room air with oxygen so it delivers an exact percentage, used when a patient needs a controlled dose.

story.title: The green adapter
story.dispatch: Interfacility transfer, 68-year-old male, COPD exacerbation, hospital to hospital, 45-minute transport.
story.body: The nurse hands you the chart and points at the patient's face: a Venturi mask with a green adapter. 'He retains CO2. The doctor wants him at exactly 28%, no more, and we've got him there. Do not swap him to a non-rebreather.' You confirm the adapter, the flow rate printed on it, and the sats: 90%, which the physician's orders say is his target. On the truck, you hook the Venturi to your own oxygen, add a humidifier bottle because it is a long ride, and keep the same adapter. Forty-five minutes later he arrives exactly as you found him. On a call like this, the most important skill was knowing what not to change.

concepts.title: Pulse oximetry
key_points: Measures the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen (SpO2) using light through a fingertip, toe, or earlobe
Normal SpO2 in a healthy person is about 95% to 100%; below 94% generally indicates hypoxia in the acutely ill
It is a tool, not a diagnosis: treat the patient, not the number

False or unreliable readings: carbon monoxide poisoning (reads falsely high), poor perfusion or shock, hypothermia, nail polish or artificial nails, bright ambient light, movement, dark or thick skin at the probe site in some devices
A patient can have a normal SpO2 and still be in respiratory distress or breathing inadequately
Always confirm a low reading with the patient's appearance and confirm a normal reading does not contradict what you see
misconceptions: Trusting a 99% reading in a patient pulled from a house fire (CO poisoning fools the sensor)
Withholding oxygen from a patient in obvious distress because the number looks fine
Treating a low number on a cold, poorly perfused finger as a true reading without checking
exam_favorites: Carbon monoxide gives a falsely high reading
Causes of inaccurate readings
Normal range and the threshold for concern

read.plain:
The pulse oximeter is the small clip you put on a fingertip. It shines light through the tissue and measures how much of the patient's hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. The number it gives, SpO2, is a percentage. Healthy people run 95 to 100%. In a sick patient, anything under 94% is a flag.

Here is the most important thing: it can lie. Carbon monoxide latches onto hemoglobin and the sensor cannot tell the difference between that and oxygen, so a CO-poisoned patient can read 99% while suffocating. Cold fingers, shock, and poor circulation give weak or wrong readings. Nail polish, artificial nails, bright lights, and a patient who will not hold still all interfere.

So you never treat the number alone. If the patient looks hypoxic, they are hypoxic until proven otherwise. If the number is low but the patient looks fine, check the probe, the finger, and the perfusion before you act on it. It is one vital sign among several, and the patient in front of you outranks it.
read.standard: Pulse oximetry estimates arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) by measuring the differential absorption of red and infrared light by oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin across a pulsatile capillary bed. Normal values are approximately 95% to 100%; readings below 94% in acutely ill patients suggest hypoxemia and typically warrant supplemental oxygen per protocol. The device cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, producing falsely normal or high readings in carbon monoxide poisoning. Accuracy is also reduced by hypoperfusion, hypothermia, vasoconstriction, motion artifact, ambient light, nail polish, and severe anemia. SpO2 reflects oxygenation, not ventilation; a patient with adequate saturation may still have inadequate ventilation and rising CO2. Clinical assessment always takes precedence over the reading.

eli_new.analogy: The pulse ox counts how many seats on the bus are full. It cannot tell you who is sitting in them.
eli_new.body:
Hemoglobin is a bus with seats for oxygen. The pulse ox counts full seats and reports a percentage. But carbon monoxide sits in the same seats, and the device counts it as a passenger. That is why a CO patient can read 99% and still be dying: the seats are full of the wrong thing.

It also needs a good signal to count at all. Cold fingers, shock, nail polish, and a patient waving their hand around all blur the picture. And even a perfectly accurate full-bus count tells you nothing about whether the patient is breathing enough to keep it full. Look at the patient first, then the number.

teach.prompt: Explain to a new EMT when you should not trust the pulse oximeter.

must_hit.point: Carbon monoxide reads falsely high
Poor perfusion or cold gives bad readings
Treat the patient, not the number

teach.model_answer: Do not trust it in carbon monoxide poisoning, because CO fills hemoglobin and the sensor reads it as oxygen, so the number looks great while the patient is hypoxic. Do not trust it on cold fingers, in shock, or with poor circulation, nail polish, bright light, or a moving patient. And never let a normal number talk you out of treating a patient who looks like they are struggling.

story.title: Ninety-nine percent
story.dispatch: Rescue 7, 35-year-old female, headache and nausea, family reports 'the whole house feels sick.'
story.body:
It is the first cold night of the year. Three people in the living room, all with headaches, one vomiting. Your partner clips the pulse ox on the patient: 99%. He looks at you like the call is nothing. You look at the space heater in the corner, then at the three sick people, and you say the word out loud: carbon monoxide. Everyone goes outside. Fire comes in with a meter and it screams in the kitchen.

All three go on non-rebreathers at 15 liters, sats 99% the whole way to the hospital, because the number was never going to tell you the truth. The heater was.

concepts.title: Oxygen targets and when not to over-oxygenate
key_points: Oxygen is a drug: it has indications, a dose, and side effects
Modern guidance is to titrate oxygen to a target SpO2 of 94% to 99% in most patients rather than giving high-flow oxygen to everyone
Give high-concentration oxygen without hesitation to any patient with signs of hypoxia, shock, respiratory distress, or inadequate breathing
Routine high-flow oxygen in patients who are not hypoxic (some heart attack and stroke patients) is no longer recommended; hyperoxia may worsen outcomes
Some chronic COPD patients who retain CO2 rely on a low-oxygen drive; titrate to a lower target (often about 88% to 92%) per protocol, but never withhold oxygen from a COPD patient in true distress
Follow local protocol; it overrides any general rule
misconceptions: 'Everyone gets 15 liters by non-rebreather' as a reflex
Withholding oxygen entirely from a hypoxic COPD patient because of the hypoxic-drive concern
Thinking more oxygen is always harmless
exam_favorites: The SpO2 target range for most patients
The COPD patient: lower target, but never withhold from a patient in distress
Why routine high-flow oxygen is no longer given to non-hypoxic cardiac and stroke patients

read.plain:
For decades every ambulance patient got a non-rebreather at 15 liters. That is not how it works anymore. Oxygen is a drug, and like any drug you give the right dose to the right patient. Too little is dangerous. Too much, it turns out, can also be.

The modern rule is simple: aim for a saturation of 94 to 99%. If the patient is below 94%, give oxygen and adjust until they are in range. If they are already in range and breathing comfortably, they do not need more. Research showed that flooding non-hypoxic heart attack and stroke patients with oxygen did not help and may have hurt, so routine high-flow oxygen for those patients is gone.

There is one group that needs extra care. Some patients with severe, long-standing COPD retain carbon dioxide, and their breathing drive has adapted to run on low oxygen. Give them too much and their breathing can slow. For these patients protocols usually set a lower target, around 88 to 92%. But this is not a reason to withhold oxygen. A COPD patient who is blue, confused, and struggling gets oxygen. You just watch closely and titrate.

And when a patient is clearly hypoxic, in shock, or in respiratory distress, none of this hesitation applies. High-concentration oxygen, now. The targets exist to stop reflex over-treatment, not to make you slow down for the patient who is dying in front of you.
read.standard: Current guidelines treat supplemental oxygen as a titratable medication with a target SpO2 of 94% to 99% for most acutely ill patients. High-concentration oxygen remains indicated for hypoxemia, shock, respiratory distress, inadequate ventilation, cardiac arrest, carbon monoxide poisoning, and other conditions per protocol. Routine high-flow oxygen in normoxic patients with acute coronary syndrome or stroke is no longer recommended, as hyperoxia is associated with vasoconstriction and increased oxidative injury without demonstrated benefit. For patients with COPD at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, a target of approximately 88% to 92% is commonly used; oxygen should still be administered to any such patient with hypoxemia or distress, with close monitoring of mental status and respiratory effort. Local protocol governs specific targets and devices.

eli_new.analogy: Oxygen is medicine, not water. You do not pour it on everyone; you dose it.
eli_new.body:
Imagine giving every patient the maximum dose of a painkiller whether they hurt or not. Nobody would do that. Oxygen used to be treated that way, and it took a lot of research to notice that some patients were worse for it.

The target of 94 to 99% is the dosing chart. Below it, give more. In it, hold steady. The COPD exception is a patient whose body is used to running a little low, so their chart says 88 to 92. But a chart never tells you to let someone suffocate. Distress means give oxygen, every time, and then adjust.

teach.prompt: Explain why we no longer put every patient on a non-rebreather, and who still gets high-flow oxygen without question.

must_hit.point: Target SpO2 94 to 99%
Too much oxygen can harm some patients
Distress, shock, hypoxia still get high-flow oxygen

teach.model_answer: Oxygen is a drug with a dose. We aim for a sat of 94 to 99% and adjust to get there, because research showed that flooding patients who were not hypoxic, like some heart attack and stroke patients, did not help and may have hurt them. That said, anyone hypoxic, in shock, or in respiratory distress still gets high-concentration oxygen right away. Some COPD patients have a lower target, around 88 to 92, but you never withhold oxygen from one who is struggling.

story.title: Ninety-six and comfortable
story.dispatch: Medic 2, 62-year-old male, chest pain, onset 20 minutes ago, alert, private residence.
story.body:
He is sitting on the couch, gray, sweaty, pressure in the center of his chest. You get him on the monitor and the pulse ox: 96%. Breathing normally, speaking in full sentences. The older EMT you rode with as a student would have had a non-rebreather on him before the door closed. You do not. You give aspirin per protocol, get the twelve-lead, and move. On the way in you check the sat again: 95%. Still in range. No oxygen.

Your partner asks about it. You tell him what you were taught: oxygen is a drug, this patient is not hypoxic, and pushing his sats to 100% would not help his heart and might make things worse. If he drops under 94, the cannula goes on. He never does.

concepts.title: Bag-valve-mask: one- and two-rescuer technique
key_points: The EMT's tool for ventilating a patient who is not breathing adequately on their own
Attach oxygen at high flow and use the reservoir; without oxygen the bag delivers room air
Two rescuers is the preferred technique: one holds the seal with both hands, the other squeezes
A one-rescuer seal uses the C-grip, thumb and index finger forming a C on the mask, remaining fingers lifting the jaw into the mask
Squeeze until you see the chest rise, then stop; chest rise is the endpoint, not bag volume
A poor mask seal is the most common reason ventilation fails
An airway adjunct and a positioned head make the bag work; the bag does not open the airway
misconceptions: Squeezing harder or faster instead of fixing the seal
Ventilating without oxygen connected
Trying to hold a seal one-handed when a second rescuer is available
Using bag volume rather than chest rise as the endpoint
exam_favorites: Two-rescuer preferred and why
The C-grip
Chest rise as the endpoint
That a bad seal, not a weak squeeze, is the usual failure

read.plain:
A bag-valve-mask is how an EMT breathes for somebody. It is a self-inflating bag, a one-way valve and a mask, and it should always have oxygen running into it with the reservoir attached. Without that, you are pushing room air.

The hard part is not the squeezing. It is the seal. If air escapes around the mask, nothing reaches the lungs no matter how hard you work. That is why two rescuers is the preferred way: one person uses both hands to hold the mask down and lift the jaw up into it, and the other squeezes the bag.

Working alone, you use the C-grip. Thumb and index finger make a C over the mask and press down; your remaining fingers hook under the bony jaw and lift it up into the mask. You are pulling the face into the mask, not mashing the mask onto the face.

Squeeze slowly and stop as soon as the chest rises. Chest rise is the whole endpoint. Squeezing more than that pushes air into the stomach.

And remember what the bag does not do. It does not open the airway. Position the head, put in an adjunct, then ventilate.
read.standard: The bag-valve-mask (BVM) provides positive-pressure ventilation for patients with absent or inadequate spontaneous breathing. The device is used with supplemental oxygen at high flow and an attached reservoir; without these it delivers approximately ambient oxygen concentration. Two-rescuer technique is preferred: one provider maintains the mask seal bilaterally while simultaneously performing a jaw lift, and the second delivers ventilations. Single-rescuer ventilation uses the C-grip, in which the thumb and index finger secure the mask while the remaining digits elevate the mandible into the mask. Adequate volume is defined by visible chest rise; excessive volume or rate produces gastric insufflation and raises the risk of regurgitation. Inadequate mask seal is the predominant cause of ineffective ventilation. The BVM does not establish airway patency: head positioning and an appropriate adjunct remain prerequisites.

eli_new.analogy: You are not pushing the mask onto the face. You are pulling the face up into the mask.
eli_new.body: New EMTs squeeze harder when ventilation is not working. Almost always the problem is at the other end. Air is leaking out around the edge of the mask, and a harder squeeze just makes a louder leak. Fix the seal, get a second pair of hands on it, and the same squeeze suddenly works.

teach.prompt: Walk a new EMT through ventilating an apneic adult with a bag-valve-mask, and tell them what to check first when it is not working.

must_hit.point: Oxygen connected with the reservoir
Two-rescuer technique is preferred
Squeeze until the chest rises and stop
A poor seal is the usual failure

teach.model_answer: Get oxygen on it at high flow with the reservoir attached, or you are just moving room air. Position the head and put in an adjunct first, because the bag does not open an airway. If there are two of you, one holds the mask down with both hands and lifts the jaw into it while the other squeezes. Alone, use the C-grip: thumb and index finger pressing the mask, the other fingers pulling the bony jaw up into it. Squeeze slowly until you see the chest rise, then stop. When it is not working, check the seal before anything else — a leak is far more likely than a weak squeeze.

story.title: Two pairs of hands
story.dispatch: Rescue 2, Engine 4 — unresponsive, not breathing normally, residence.
story.body:
You are alone at the head with the bag and it is not going well. The chest barely moves and you can hear air hissing out by his cheek every time you squeeze.

Engine 4 comes through the door. Their firefighter drops to the head, takes the mask in both hands, pulls the jaw up into it, and nods. You squeeze the same bag with the same pressure and the chest rises properly for the first time.

Nothing changed except the seal.

concepts.title: Ventilation rates by age and situation
key_points: Ventilation rate depends on the patient's age, whether there is a pulse, and whether an advanced airway is in place
An adult in respiratory arrest with a pulse is ventilated at roughly one breath every 5 to 6 seconds
Children and infants are ventilated faster than adults, and the exact rate has changed between guideline editions
Ventilating too fast is actively harmful: it inflates the stomach and reduces blood return to the heart
Each breath is delivered over about a second, just until the chest rises
misconceptions: Ventilating as fast as adrenaline suggests rather than counting
Using the same rate for an adult and an infant
Believing that more ventilation is always better
exam_favorites: The adult rescue-breathing interval
That pediatric rates are faster
Why hyperventilation is harmful
One second per breath, to chest rise

read.plain:
Rate matters as much as technique. Too slow and the patient stays hypoxic. Too fast and you actively cause harm, which surprises people.

For an adult who has a pulse but is not breathing, the commonly taught interval is one breath every 5 to 6 seconds. Say it out loud as you go — squeeze, two, three, four, five.

Children and infants get ventilated faster than adults, because their normal rates are faster. The exact numbers have been revised between guideline editions, so use the figure your current text and protocol give rather than a number you half-remember.

Deliver each breath over about a second, and only until the chest rises. A fast, hard squeeze forces air past the esophagus into the stomach.

The reason to care about going too fast is not just gastric distention. Every positive-pressure breath raises the pressure inside the chest, and that pressure works against blood returning to the heart. Ventilate too fast and you can drop the very output you are trying to support.
read.standard: Ventilation rate is determined by patient age, the presence of a pulse, and whether an advanced airway is in place. For the adult in respiratory arrest with a perfusing rhythm, ventilation is commonly taught at approximately one breath every 5 to 6 seconds. Pediatric patients are ventilated at higher rates reflecting their higher baseline respiratory rates; the specific intervals have been revised across guideline editions and must be taken from the current standard rather than recalled. Each ventilation is delivered over approximately one second to visible chest rise. Excessive ventilation rate or volume produces gastric insufflation with attendant regurgitation risk, and raises intrathoracic pressure sufficiently to impede venous return and reduce cardiac output. Hyperventilation is therefore not a benign error.

eli_new.analogy: Every squeeze is a small squeeze on the heart as well as the lungs. Do it too often and you strangle the pump you are trying to help.
eli_new.body: It feels wrong to slow down when somebody is not breathing. But each breath you push in raises the pressure inside the chest, and the heart fills between breaths. Pile the breaths on top of each other and there is never a low-pressure moment for blood to come back. Counting out loud is what keeps you honest.

teach.prompt: Explain to a new EMT how fast to ventilate an adult who has a pulse but is not breathing, and why going faster is not better.

must_hit.point: About one breath every 5 to 6 seconds for an adult
Each breath over about a second, to chest rise
Too fast inflates the stomach
Too fast reduces blood return to the heart

teach.model_answer: For an adult with a pulse who is not breathing, the commonly taught interval is one breath every 5 to 6 seconds, delivered over about a second, just until the chest rises. Count out loud, because adrenaline makes everyone go faster than they think. Going faster is not better: extra volume and extra rate push air into the stomach, and every positive-pressure breath raises the pressure inside the chest, which works against blood coming back to the heart. Hyperventilating can lower the output you are trying to support. Children and infants are ventilated faster than adults, but take that number from your current text because it has changed between editions.

story.title: Counting out loud
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — unresponsive, agonal breathing, pulse present.
story.body:
Your partner is on the bag and going far too fast, one breath on top of the next, because that is what your hands want to do when somebody is dying in front of you.

The medic arriving says one word: count. Your partner starts saying it out loud — squeeze, two, three, four, five — and the rhythm settles. The stomach stops rising under the shirt.

Nobody squeezed harder. They just stopped stacking the breaths.

concepts.title: Signs of adequate artificial ventilation
key_points: The chest rises and falls visibly with each ventilation
The rate is appropriate for the patient's age and situation
Heart rate and skin colour improve as oxygenation improves
Signs of inadequate ventilation: no chest rise, a rate that is too slow or too fast, and a stomach that is inflating
Ventilation is assessed continuously, not confirmed once and forgotten
misconceptions: Confirming chest rise on the first breath and never looking again
Judging adequacy by how hard the bag feels rather than by the patient
Ignoring a rising abdomen
exam_favorites: Chest rise as the primary sign
Rising stomach as a sign of a problem
That ventilation is reassessed continuously

read.plain:
Once you start ventilating, the question becomes: is it working? You answer it from the patient, not from the equipment.

The first thing is chest rise. It should go up and come down with every squeeze, visibly, the way a normal breath looks. Not a twitch, not a heave.

The second is rate. Appropriate for the age, steady, not stacked on top of itself.

Then watch the patient change. As oxygen gets in, colour improves and a fast heart rate often begins to settle. Those are downstream signs and they take time, but they tell you it is working.

Now the failures. No chest rise means the air is going somewhere other than the lungs, usually past a bad seal or into a blocked airway. A stomach that is visibly inflating means air is going down the esophagus, which means too much volume, too much speed, or an airway that is not properly open.

And this is not a one-time check. Seals slip, heads move, patients vomit. Keep looking.
read.standard: Adequate artificial ventilation is assessed from the patient rather than the device. The primary indicator is visible bilateral chest rise and fall with each delivered breath, of a volume comparable to a normal spontaneous breath. Rate must be appropriate to age and clinical situation. Secondary indicators include improvement in skin colour and normalisation of a previously elevated heart rate as oxygenation improves. Indicators of inadequate ventilation include absent or minimal chest rise, a rate that is too slow or too rapid, and progressive gastric distention, which signals esophageal insufflation from excessive volume, excessive rate, or incomplete airway opening. Assessment is continuous: mask seal, head position and airway patency all degrade over time, and vomiting may occur at any point.

eli_new.analogy: The patient is the gauge, not the bag.
eli_new.body: It is easy to get absorbed in the equipment — how the bag feels, whether the reservoir is full. None of that tells you whether air is reaching lungs. Look at the chest. Look at the belly. Look at the colour. The patient tells you the truth.

teach.prompt: Tell a new EMT how they know their ventilations are working, and what the warning signs look like.

must_hit.point: Visible chest rise and fall with each breath
Appropriate rate for age
Improving colour and heart rate
A rising stomach means air is going the wrong way

teach.model_answer: You judge it from the patient. The chest should rise and fall visibly with every squeeze, about like a normal breath, and the rate should suit the patient's age without breaths stacking up. Over the next minutes, colour should improve and a fast heart rate often settles. The warnings are the opposite: no chest rise means the air is not reaching the lungs, usually a seal or airway problem, and a stomach that keeps inflating means you are pushing air down the esophagus from too much volume, too much speed, or an airway that is not properly open. Keep checking — seals slip and heads move.

story.title: The rising shirt
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — cardiac arrest, bystander CPR in progress.
story.body:
Four minutes into the code, somebody notices the patient's shirt is tight across his stomach in a way it was not when you arrived.

Chest rise had been marginal for a while and the person on the bag had been compensating by squeezing more. All of that extra volume had been going into the stomach.

Repositioning the head and fixing the seal got the chest moving again with less pressure, not more.

concepts.title: Gastric distention and cricoid pressure
key_points: Gastric distention is air forced into the stomach by ventilation that is too fast, too forceful, or through a partly obstructed airway
A distended stomach pushes up against the diaphragm and makes ventilation harder
It substantially raises the risk of regurgitation and aspiration
The fix is technique: slow down, use less volume, and make sure the airway is properly open
Cricoid pressure was historically taught to prevent it and is no longer routinely recommended
Suction must be immediately available whenever you are ventilating
misconceptions: Trying to press the air out of a distended stomach
Continuing the same technique and accepting distention as unavoidable
Believing cricoid pressure is still standard practice
exam_favorites: What causes gastric distention
Why it matters
That cricoid pressure is historical
That the correction is technique, not pressure

read.plain:
Air takes the path of least resistance. If the airway is not fully open, or you squeeze too fast or too hard, some of that air goes down the esophagus into the stomach instead of into the lungs.

You will see it as a stomach that gets progressively bigger. Two things follow. First, the inflated stomach pushes up on the diaphragm and gives the lungs less room, so ventilation gets harder and you are tempted to squeeze harder still. Second, and worse, a full stomach is much more likely to empty itself back up into the throat. Now you are ventilating through vomit.

The fix is not force. It is technique. Slow the rate. Use only the volume that makes the chest rise. Recheck that the head is positioned and the adjunct is doing its job.

Do not press on the abdomen to push the air out. That is how you cause the regurgitation you are trying to avoid.

For years, pressure on the cricoid cartilage was taught to occlude the esophagus and prevent this. It is no longer routinely recommended. Know what it is, know it was standard, and know that current practice has moved away from it.
read.standard: Gastric distention results from insufflation of air into the esophagus and stomach during positive-pressure ventilation, and is caused by excessive ventilation rate, excessive tidal volume, or incomplete airway opening. Progressive distention elevates the diaphragm, reducing pulmonary compliance and making subsequent ventilation more difficult, and markedly increases the risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Management is corrective technique: reduce rate and volume, deliver only to visible chest rise, and reconfirm airway positioning and adjunct placement. Manual abdominal pressure to decompress the stomach is not performed, as it precipitates regurgitation. Cricoid pressure (the Sellick maneuver), historically taught to occlude the esophagus during ventilation, is no longer routinely recommended; EMTs should recognise the term and its historical role while following current guidance. Suction must remain immediately available throughout positive-pressure ventilation.

eli_new.analogy: You are filling two bags through one opening. Push too hard and the wrong bag fills.
eli_new.body: Air goes wherever it is easiest to go. Lungs are easy when the airway is open and you squeeze gently. Make the airway harder to get into, or push harder than the lungs want, and the stomach becomes the easier option. It is that simple, and the answer is always to make the lungs easier rather than to push harder.

teach.prompt: Explain what causes gastric distention during ventilation, why it is dangerous, and what you do about it.

must_hit.point: Caused by too fast, too forceful, or a partly obstructed airway
Pushes on the diaphragm and makes ventilation harder
Raises the risk of vomiting and aspiration
Fixed by slowing down and reopening the airway, not by pressing on the abdomen

teach.model_answer: It happens when air goes down the esophagus instead of the trachea, which comes from ventilating too fast, using too much volume, or working through an airway that is not properly open. The stomach fills, pushes up on the diaphragm, and ventilation gets harder — which tempts you to squeeze harder and makes it worse. The real danger is that a full stomach regurgitates, and then you are pushing vomit into the lungs. Fix it by slowing down, giving only enough volume for chest rise, and rechecking the head position and adjunct. Never press on the abdomen to force the air out. Cricoid pressure used to be taught for this and is no longer routinely recommended.

story.title: Harder is not better
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — unresponsive, not breathing, apartment.
story.body:
The chest was barely moving, so the newer EMT on the bag did what feels natural and squeezed harder and faster. Ten minutes later the patient's abdomen was visibly domed and the bag felt stiff in his hand.

The medic took the mask, repositioned the head, seated the adjunct properly, and handed it back with one instruction: half as fast, half as hard.

The chest started rising properly. The bag got easier, not harder.

concepts.title: CPAP: indications, contraindications, setup
key_points: Continuous positive airway pressure holds the airways and alveoli open through the whole breathing cycle
For an awake patient who is breathing on their own but working hard and staying hypoxic
Classic indications include pulmonary edema from heart failure and a COPD exacerbation, per local protocol
The patient must be awake enough to cooperate, follow instructions and protect their own airway
Contraindicated in respiratory or cardiac arrest, in a patient who cannot protect their airway, and in a patient who is vomiting
Hypotension and suspected pneumothorax are contraindications because the pressure impedes venous return
Talk the patient through it: the mask is tight and frightening, and tolerance decides whether it works
misconceptions: Putting CPAP on a patient who is not breathing adequately on their own
Using it on an obtunded patient who cannot protect the airway
Applying the mask without coaching the patient through it
Treating it as a substitute for ventilation
exam_favorites: Awake and breathing on their own is the entry requirement
Arrest and inability to protect the airway are absolute contraindications
Why hypotension matters
That coaching determines tolerance

read.plain:
CPAP is a tight mask that delivers continuous pressure, so the patient is breathing against a constant push. That pressure holds small airways and alveoli open at the end of each breath instead of letting them collapse, and in pulmonary edema it helps push fluid back out of the air spaces.

The patient has to be doing the breathing. CPAP supports a patient who is working hard and losing; it does not breathe for anyone. Awake, able to follow instructions, able to protect their own airway.

The classic candidates are heart failure with pulmonary edema, and COPD exacerbations, within your protocol.

The contraindications follow from the same logic. Respiratory or cardiac arrest means they cannot breathe against it, so they need ventilation instead. A patient who cannot protect their airway, or who is vomiting, will aspirate behind a sealed mask. Low blood pressure is a problem because the pressure in the chest works against blood returning to the heart. Suspected pneumothorax is a problem for obvious reasons.

Finally, the human part. A tight mask blowing air at a frightened, breathless person feels like drowning. Explain it, hold it gently against the face before strapping, and keep talking. Most CPAP failures are tolerance failures.
read.standard: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers a constant positive pressure throughout the respiratory cycle, maintaining alveolar and small-airway patency at end-expiration, increasing functional residual capacity, and in cardiogenic pulmonary edema promoting movement of fluid out of the alveolar space. It is indicated for the spontaneously breathing patient with increased work of breathing and persistent hypoxia, classically in acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema and in COPD exacerbation, subject to local protocol. The patient must be alert enough to cooperate with the mask, follow instruction, and protect the airway. Contraindications include respiratory or cardiac arrest, inadequate spontaneous ventilation, inability to protect the airway, active vomiting, hypotension, and suspected pneumothorax; elevated intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return and may precipitate hemodynamic compromise. Coaching is a determinant of success, as mask intolerance is a common cause of failure.

eli_new.analogy: It is a stiff breeze against a door that keeps swinging shut — the door stays open because the pressure never stops.
eli_new.body: Picture the smallest air sacs collapsing a little at the end of every breath, so the next breath has to pop them open again. That is exhausting. CPAP keeps a constant pressure so they never fully close. The patient stops spending energy reopening their lungs and can use it on actually breathing.

teach.prompt: Explain which patient you would put on CPAP, which patient you would not, and why the not-list looks the way it does.

must_hit.point: Awake, breathing on their own, working hard and hypoxic
Classic uses are pulmonary edema and COPD
Not in arrest or inadequate breathing
Not if they cannot protect the airway or are vomiting
Hypotension is a contraindication

teach.model_answer: CPAP is for an awake patient who is breathing on their own but working hard and staying hypoxic — classically pulmonary edema from heart failure, or a COPD exacerbation, within protocol. They have to be able to cooperate and protect their own airway, because the mask seals tight. You do not use it on someone in arrest or breathing inadequately, because CPAP supports breathing rather than replacing it, and that patient needs ventilation. You do not use it on someone who cannot protect their airway or who is vomiting, because they will aspirate behind the mask. Hypotension rules it out because the pressure in the chest works against blood returning to the heart, and a suspected pneumothorax rules it out too. And you coach them through it — most failures are the patient pulling the mask off.

story.title: Talk them into it
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 78-year-old female, difficulty breathing, third floor.
story.body:
She is upright at the edge of the bed, speaking two words at a time, wet-sounding, terrified. Her sat is low and she is using every muscle she has.

Your partner holds the CPAP mask a few inches from her face first, lets her feel the air, and explains what it will feel like. Then against the face without straps. Then straps.

For the first thirty seconds she fights it and tries to pull it away. Your partner keeps a hand on her shoulder and keeps talking. By the time you are in the elevator she is taking slower, deeper breaths and saying whole sentences.

do.prompt: Sort each patient: is CPAP appropriate?

Unresponsive and apneic

Actively vomiting
Drowsy, will not follow instructions, cannot protect the airway
Breathing hard with a systolic pressure far below normal

concepts.title: Assisting a patient who is breathing inadequately
key_points: For a patient who is breathing but not moving enough air: too slow, too shallow, or tiring out
You add volume to the breaths they are already taking rather than replacing them
Time your squeeze to begin as the patient starts to inhale
Squeezing against a patient's exhalation fights them and delivers nothing
If their own effort fades, this becomes full ventilation
A patient breathing 30 shallow times a minute can be moving less useful air than one breathing 12 deeply
misconceptions: Waiting for a patient to stop breathing entirely before helping
Squeezing on your own rhythm rather than theirs
Judging adequacy by rate alone
exam_favorites: Timing the squeeze to the patient's inhalation
Rate alone does not equal adequacy
The transition from assisting to full ventilation

read.plain:
There is a patient between 'breathing fine' and 'not breathing at all', and they are easy to miss. They are breathing — often fast — but each breath is shallow and moves almost nothing useful. Or they are breathing slowly and deeply enough per breath but nowhere near often enough. Either way the total air moved is not sustaining them.

This patient does not need you to take over. They need you to add to what they are already doing.

Explain what you are going to do if they are awake enough to hear it. Get the mask sealed. Then watch their chest, and as they begin to inhale, squeeze. You are topping up a breath they started.

Getting this wrong is the common failure. If you squeeze on your own count, sooner or later you are pushing air in while they are pushing it out. You fight each other, nothing goes in, and air ends up in the stomach.

Watch for the moment their effort fades. When it does, you stop assisting and start doing all of it.
read.standard: Assisted ventilation is indicated for the patient with spontaneous but inadequate respiration, whether from inadequate rate, inadequate tidal volume, or exhaustion. The technique augments rather than replaces the patient's own effort: after establishing a mask seal, the provider initiates each squeeze synchronously with the onset of the patient's inspiration, adding volume to the breath already beginning. Asynchronous ventilation delivered against active exhalation is ineffective and promotes gastric insufflation. Adequacy is assessed by total air movement rather than rate alone: a patient breathing rapidly and shallowly may achieve substantially less effective alveolar ventilation than one breathing more slowly with adequate tidal volume. Deterioration of the patient's own respiratory effort mandates transition from assisted to full positive-pressure ventilation.

eli_new.analogy: You are not rowing for them. You are pulling on the same oar, at the same moment they do.
eli_new.body: The instinct is to establish your own rhythm and make the patient fit it. Do the opposite. Watch their chest, wait for the start of their breath, and squeeze then. You are helping a breath they already decided to take, which is why timing matters more than force.

teach.prompt: Explain how you assist ventilations on a patient who is breathing but inadequately, and what you are watching for while you do it.

must_hit.point: For breathing that is too slow, too shallow, or tiring
Time the squeeze to the start of their own inhalation
Squeezing against exhalation fights them
Move to full ventilation if their effort fades

teach.model_answer: This is the patient who is breathing but not moving enough air — too slow, too shallow, or simply running out of energy. You are adding to their breaths, not replacing them. Tell them what you are doing if they can hear you, get a good seal, watch the chest, and start your squeeze exactly as they begin to breathe in. If you squeeze on your own rhythm you will eventually be pushing in while they are pushing out, which achieves nothing and fills the stomach. Judge them on total air moved, not rate — fast and shallow can be worse than slow and deep. And watch for their effort fading, because that is the moment you stop assisting and start doing all the breathing for them.

story.title: Fast and going nowhere
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 61-year-old male, difficulty breathing, worsening.
story.body:
He is breathing about thirty times a minute and at first glance that looks like a lot of breathing. Then you watch his chest and it barely moves. He cannot finish a word.

Your partner seals the mask and starts squeezing with him, catching the beginning of each breath. The first two are mistimed and you can hear them fight. The third lands with him and his chest actually rises.

Six minutes later his rate has come down to the low twenties and he manages a short sentence.

concepts.title: Stoma and tracheostomy ventilation
key_points: A stoma is a surgical opening in the front of the neck that the patient breathes through directly
Ventilate at the stoma, not at the mouth and nose
A pediatric or infant mask often seals better over a stoma than an adult mask
If air escapes from the mouth and nose while you ventilate the stoma, seal them and continue at the stoma
Secretions block stomas readily; suction may be needed before ventilation will work
Head position does not open a stoma; the airway starts at the neck
misconceptions: Ventilating at the face when the patient has a stoma
Assuming head positioning will help
Forgetting that the mouth and nose may need sealing
exam_favorites: Ventilate at the stoma
Sealing the mouth and nose when air escapes
That positioning the head does not apply

read.plain:
Some patients breathe through a hole in the front of the neck. It may be from a laryngectomy or a tracheostomy, and it may or may not have a tube in it. What matters to you is that their airway starts at the neck, not at the mouth.

So ventilate there. Put the mask over the stoma, not over the face. An infant or pediatric mask usually seals better on a neck than a full-size adult mask does.

If you are ventilating the stoma and you hear or feel air coming out of the mouth and nose, that patient still has a connection between the two. Seal the mouth and nose — a hand works — and keep going at the stoma.

Stomas block with secretions easily. If ventilation will not go in, suction may be the answer before anything else.

And unlearn one reflex. Tilting the head does nothing here. There is no tongue between your air and their lungs. The airway starts at the opening in front of you.
read.standard: A stoma is a surgical opening in the anterior neck through which the patient breathes, resulting from laryngectomy or tracheostomy, and may or may not contain a tube. Positive-pressure ventilation is delivered directly at the stoma rather than at the face. A pediatric or infant mask frequently achieves a better seal over the stoma than an adult mask. Where the upper airway remains patent, air delivered at the stoma may escape through the mouth and nose; these should be sealed manually while ventilation continues at the stoma. Stomas obstruct readily with secretions, and suctioning may be required before ventilation becomes effective. Head positioning maneuvers do not contribute to patency in the stoma patient, as the airway is entered distal to the oropharynx.

eli_new.analogy: Their front door has been moved to the side of the house. Knocking at the old one does nothing.
eli_new.body: Everything you have learned about airways assumes the air goes in at the face. This patient's air goes in at the neck. Once you accept that, the rest follows: put the mask where the air goes, seal anywhere it leaks, and forget about tilting the head.

teach.prompt: Explain how ventilating a patient with a stoma differs from ventilating anyone else.

must_hit.point: Ventilate at the stoma, not the face
A smaller pediatric or infant mask often seals better
Seal the mouth and nose if air escapes there
Head positioning does not open a stoma

teach.model_answer: Their airway starts at the neck, so the mask goes over the stoma rather than the face. A pediatric or infant mask usually seals better on a neck than an adult one. If you feel or hear air escaping from the mouth and nose while you ventilate, their upper airway is still connected — seal the mouth and nose with your hand and keep ventilating at the stoma. Stomas clog with secretions, so if nothing is going in, suction before you try harder. And tilting the head does nothing for this patient, because there is no tongue between your air and their lungs.

story.title: The wrong door
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — unresponsive male, home care patient, family on scene.
story.body:
The new EMT had the mask on his face and was getting nothing. His daughter said, quietly, he doesn't breathe through there.

There was a stoma at the base of his neck, half-covered by a dressing. Your partner swapped to a pediatric mask, sealed it over the stoma, and the chest rose on the first squeeze.

On the second squeeze you felt air on your wrist from his mouth, so you cupped a hand over his mouth and nose, and it all went where it was supposed to.

concepts.title: Capnography at the EMT level
key_points: Capnography measures the carbon dioxide in exhaled breath, and shows it as a number and a waveform
A normal end-tidal carbon dioxide is roughly 35 to 45 mmHg
It confirms that air is actually moving in and out, which pulse oximetry does not
A rising number can mean ventilation is too slow; a falling number can mean it is too fast
In cardiac arrest a suddenly rising value can be the first sign of return of circulation
It reflects ventilation, while pulse oximetry reflects oxygenation; they answer different questions
misconceptions: Treating capnography and pulse oximetry as interchangeable
Reading the number without looking at the waveform
Assuming a good pulse oximetry reading means ventilation is adequate
exam_favorites: The normal end-tidal range
Ventilation versus oxygenation
What a rising value in arrest suggests
That it confirms air movement

read.plain:
Pulse oximetry tells you how much oxygen is on the blood. Capnography tells you whether air is actually moving. They are different questions, and a patient can look fine on one while failing the other.

Capnography samples exhaled breath and reports the carbon dioxide at the end of each exhalation, normally somewhere around 35 to 45 mmHg. It draws a waveform as well as a number, and the shape carries information the number alone does not.

Because carbon dioxide only appears in exhaled air if air is being exhaled, a waveform is proof that ventilation is happening. That is why it is the standard confirmation that a breathing circuit is working.

The number moves with ventilation. Ventilate too slowly and carbon dioxide accumulates and the number climbs. Ventilate too fast and you blow it off and the number falls — which is one more reason not to hyperventilate.

In cardiac arrest it earns its keep. The value reflects how much blood is being returned to the lungs, so a sudden climb during CPR is often the first sign that circulation has come back, before anyone finds a pulse.
read.standard: Capnography measures carbon dioxide in exhaled gas, reported as an end-tidal value (EtCO2) with an accompanying waveform. The normal range is approximately 35 to 45 mmHg. Because exhaled CO2 is present only when gas is actually being exhaled, waveform capnography provides direct confirmation of ventilation and of circuit integrity, information that pulse oximetry cannot supply: capnography reflects ventilation while oximetry reflects oxygenation. EtCO2 varies inversely with minute ventilation, rising with hypoventilation and falling with hyperventilation, providing real-time feedback on ventilation rate. During cardiac arrest, EtCO2 reflects pulmonary blood flow and therefore the effectiveness of chest compressions; an abrupt sustained rise commonly precedes detection of a palpable pulse and is a recognised early indicator of return of spontaneous circulation. Waveform morphology carries diagnostic information beyond the numeric value.

eli_new.analogy: Pulse oximetry tells you what is in the tank. Capnography tells you whether the engine is actually running.
eli_new.body: A patient can have a reassuring oxygen saturation for minutes after they stop ventilating properly, because the oxygen already on board takes time to be used. Capnography does not have that lag: if no air is moving, there is no exhaled carbon dioxide, and the waveform flatlines straight away.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between what pulse oximetry tells you and what capnography tells you, and what a rising or falling number means during ventilation.

must_hit.point: Normal end-tidal CO2 is about 35 to 45 mmHg
Capnography shows ventilation, oximetry shows oxygenation
Rising means too slow, falling means too fast
A sudden rise in arrest suggests return of circulation

teach.model_answer: Pulse oximetry tells you how much oxygen is loaded onto the blood; capnography tells you whether air is actually moving in and out. A normal end-tidal carbon dioxide is roughly 35 to 45 mmHg, shown as a number and a waveform, and the waveform itself is proof that ventilation is happening. The number tracks ventilation: too slow and carbon dioxide builds up so the number climbs, too fast and you blow it off so the number falls. In cardiac arrest the value reflects blood flow through the lungs, so a sudden sustained rise during CPR is often the first sign circulation has come back, before anyone can feel a pulse.

story.title: The number moved first
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — cardiac arrest, CPR in progress on arrival.
story.body:
Nine minutes in, compressions continuous, nobody has felt anything. The medic is watching the capnography value more than the monitor.

It had been sitting low. Then it climbed, and kept climbing, and did not fall back.

At the next rhythm check there was a pulse. The number had told them almost a minute before anyone's fingers did.

concepts.title: Asthma
key_points: Three things happen at once: the airways spasm, they swell, and they fill with mucus
The trouble is getting air OUT, which is why wheezing is heard mostly on exhalation
Wheezing means air is still moving; a silent chest in a patient working hard is far worse
Accessory muscle use, tripod position and an inability to speak in full sentences mark a severe attack
Treatment at the EMT level is oxygen, calm, and assisting with the patient's own prescribed inhaler per protocol
Fatigue in a patient who has been fighting for a long time is an ominous sign
misconceptions: Taking a quiet chest as improvement
Treating wheezing as always mild
Rushing a frightened asthmatic, which worsens the attack
Assuming every wheeze is asthma
exam_favorites: Wheezing on exhalation and why
The silent chest
Speech in sentences as a severity marker

read.plain:
Asthma is three problems at once in the small airways. The muscle around them squeezes down, the lining swells, and mucus fills what is left. The passage narrows from every direction.

Air can still be pulled in, because inhaling pulls the airways open. Getting it back out is the problem, because exhaling squeezes them further shut. That is why an asthmatic wheezes mostly on the way out, and why they end up with air trapped in a chest that is already full.

Judge severity by what they can do, not by how loud they are. Can they speak a full sentence? Are they using neck and shoulder muscles? Are they sitting bolt upright with their hands on their knees? And here is the one that catches people out: a chest that has gone quiet in a patient who is still clearly fighting is not improving. It means almost nothing is moving at all.

Your treatment is oxygen, calm, and helping them use the inhaler they already have, within your protocol. Calm matters more than it sounds. Panic makes breathing faster and shallower, which is exactly wrong for a patient who cannot exhale.
read.standard: Asthma is reversible lower-airway obstruction produced by bronchospasm, mucosal inflammation and mucus plugging occurring simultaneously. Because airway calibre increases during inspiration and decreases during expiration, obstruction is predominantly expiratory, producing expiratory wheezing and air trapping with progressive hyperinflation. Severity is assessed clinically: ability to speak in complete sentences, accessory muscle use, positioning, level of consciousness and fatigue. Audible wheezing indicates air movement; a markedly diminished or silent chest in a patient with increased work of breathing indicates severe obstruction with minimal airflow and is an ominous finding rather than an improvement. Prehospital EMT management comprises supplemental oxygen, minimising exertion and anxiety, and assisting with the patient's prescribed bronchodilator in accordance with protocol.

eli_new.analogy: Breathing in opens the tube a little; breathing out squeezes it shut. That is why the air gets stuck on the way out.
eli_new.body: Everyone assumes trouble breathing means trouble getting air in. With asthma it is the opposite. Inhaling actually widens the little airways slightly, so air goes in. Exhaling narrows them, so air gets trapped. The patient ends up with a chest full of stale air and no room for a fresh breath.

teach.prompt: Explain to a new EMT what is physically happening in an asthma attack, and how they should judge how bad it is.

must_hit.point: Bronchospasm, swelling and mucus together
Trouble is getting air out, wheezing on exhalation
A silent chest is worse, not better
Judge by speech, accessory muscles, position

teach.model_answer: Three things happen at once in the small airways: the muscle around them spasms, the lining swells, and mucus fills the space. Getting air in is possible because inhaling widens them slightly, but getting it out is the problem, so you hear wheezing on the way out and air gets trapped. Judge severity by what the patient can do — can they finish a sentence, are they using neck and shoulder muscles, are they tripoding, are they exhausted. And do not be reassured by a quiet chest in a patient who is clearly still fighting: that means almost no air is moving. Your treatment is oxygen, keeping them calm, and assisting with their own prescribed inhaler per protocol.

story.title: The quiet that was not calm
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 19-year-old female, difficulty breathing, known asthmatic, college dormitory.
story.body:
She was wheezing loudly when the first crew arrived. Twenty minutes later, on the way to the truck, the wheezing had stopped.

The new EMT said she sounded better. The medic put a hand on her shoulder, looked at her neck muscles still straining and her eyes wide, and moved her straight to the front of the queue.

She had not improved. She had stopped moving enough air to make a sound.

concepts.title: COPD: emphysema and chronic bronchitis
key_points: Chronic, irreversible lung disease, usually from long-term smoking
Emphysema destroys the alveolar walls, so there is less surface to exchange gas and the lungs lose their recoil
Chronic bronchitis is long-term inflammation and mucus production in the airways
Most patients have features of both rather than one cleanly
Barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, home oxygen and a long smoking history are the recognisable picture
These patients live short of breath; what matters is how this compares with their normal
Do not withhold oxygen from a hypoxic COPD patient who needs it
misconceptions: Withholding oxygen from a hypoxic COPD patient out of a half-remembered rule
Comparing the patient to a healthy person rather than to their own baseline
Assuming every COPD patient is the same
exam_favorites: Emphysema versus chronic bronchitis
Baseline comparison
Oxygen is not withheld from a hypoxic patient

read.plain:
COPD is the long-term damage left behind by years of irritation, almost always smoking. It comes in two flavours that usually travel together.

Emphysema is destruction. The walls between the tiny air sacs break down, so instead of many small sacs with a lot of surface area you get fewer large ones with much less. The lungs also lose their springiness, so exhaling stops being passive and becomes work. That is where pursed-lip breathing comes from — the patient is making back-pressure to hold their airways open as they exhale.

Chronic bronchitis is inflammation and mucus. The airways are permanently irritated, swollen, and producing far more mucus than they should, so the patient coughs and brings things up for months at a time, year after year.

Most real patients are a mix. What you will actually see is a barrel-shaped chest, pursed lips, a long smoking history, home oxygen in the corner, and a person who is always a little short of breath.

That last part is the key to assessing them. The question is never 'is this patient short of breath' — they always are. It is 'how does today compare to their normal?' Ask them, or ask whoever lives with them.

One more thing. You may hear a rule about oxygen being dangerous in COPD. Do not let it stop you giving oxygen to a hypoxic patient in front of you. A hypoxic patient needs oxygen.
read.standard: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease encompasses emphysema and chronic bronchitis, most commonly resulting from long-term tobacco exposure. Emphysema is characterised by destruction of alveolar septa, producing reduced gas-exchange surface area and loss of elastic recoil, which converts expiration from a passive to an active process; pursed-lip breathing generates back-pressure that maintains small-airway patency during expiration. Chronic bronchitis is characterised by chronic airway inflammation and mucus hypersecretion with productive cough. Most patients demonstrate overlapping features. Clinical recognition includes barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, tripod positioning, extensive smoking history and home oxygen use. Assessment is referenced to the patient's own baseline rather than to a healthy norm. Supplemental oxygen is not withheld from the hypoxic COPD patient.

eli_new.analogy: Emphysema is the wall between rooms knocked out. Chronic bronchitis is the hallway full of furniture.
eli_new.body: Two different kinds of damage. One destroys the surfaces where gas exchange happens and leaves the lung floppy. The other clogs and narrows the tubes leading to them. Smoking does both, which is why most patients have a bit of each.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between emphysema and chronic bronchitis, and how you decide whether a COPD patient is having a bad day.

must_hit.point: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and loses recoil
Chronic bronchitis is inflammation and mucus
Assess against the patient's own baseline
Do not withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient

teach.model_answer: Emphysema is destruction: the walls between the air sacs break down, so there is less surface for gas exchange and the lung loses its springiness, which makes exhaling hard work and drives pursed-lip breathing. Chronic bronchitis is inflammation and mucus in the airways, with a long-standing productive cough. Most patients have both. Because they are always somewhat short of breath, the assessment question is how today compares with their own normal — ask them or their family. And do not withhold oxygen from a COPD patient who is hypoxic in front of you.

story.title: Worse than her Tuesdays
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 71-year-old female, difficulty breathing, home oxygen in use.
story.body:
She is on two litres at home and always has been. She is pursed-lip breathing, barrel-chested, and can manage about four words at a time.

The new EMT is not sure whether that is bad, because she has never seen her before. Her daughter answers it in one sentence: on a normal Tuesday she walks to the kitchen and back.

Today she cannot get from the chair to the door. That is the finding.

concepts.title: Pneumonia
key_points: An infection of the lung tissue itself, not just the airways
Fluid and pus fill the air sacs in the affected area, so that part of the lung stops exchanging gas
Fever, chills, a productive cough and chest discomfort that is worse on breathing in
Abnormal sounds are often localised to one area rather than heard throughout
Common and dangerous at the extremes of age, and in patients who are already unwell
EMT care is oxygen, position of comfort, and transport; the infection itself is treated in hospital
misconceptions: Expecting pneumonia to sound the same in both lungs
Dismissing it in an elderly patient who presents only with confusion and weakness
Confusing the crackles of pneumonia with those of pulmonary edema without considering the whole picture
exam_favorites: That findings are often one-sided
Fever distinguishing it from most other causes
Atypical presentation in the elderly

read.plain:
Pneumonia is an infection in the lung tissue itself. The air sacs in the affected area fill with fluid and pus, and that region simply stops doing its job. The rest of the lung carries on.

That is why the findings are often lopsided. You may hear crackles or diminished sound over one area and something close to normal elsewhere, which is a useful clue.

The infection part shows itself as fever and chills, a cough that brings something up, and chest discomfort that gets worse when they breathe in. Put together with shortness of breath, that picture is fairly characteristic.

Be careful at the extremes of age. An older patient with pneumonia may not have an impressive fever or cough at all. They may simply be confused, weak, off their food, and falling over. Pneumonia is a common reason an elderly patient is suddenly 'not themselves'.

Your job is oxygen if they need it, a position they can breathe in, and transport. The antibiotics happen somewhere else.
read.standard: Pneumonia is infection of the pulmonary parenchyma in which alveoli in the affected region fill with inflammatory exudate, producing localised impairment of gas exchange. Because involvement is typically regional rather than global, auscultatory findings are frequently unilateral or focal, with crackles or diminished breath sounds over the affected area. Characteristic features include fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic chest discomfort and dyspnea. Presentation in elderly patients is frequently atypical, with altered mental status, generalised weakness, reduced oral intake or falls in the absence of prominent fever or cough; pneumonia is a common cause of acute functional decline in this group. Prehospital management is supportive: supplemental oxygen as indicated, position of comfort and transport.

eli_new.analogy: One neighbourhood of the lung has flooded. The rest of the city is fine, which is why it sounds different in one place.
eli_new.body: Most breathing problems affect the whole lung at once — asthma narrows everything, heart failure floods everything. Pneumonia usually hits one region. If what you hear on one side is clearly different from the other, that asymmetry is telling you something.

teach.prompt: Explain what pneumonia does to the lung, what you would expect to find, and why an elderly patient might not look like the textbook.

must_hit.point: Infection filling air sacs in part of the lung
Fever, chills, productive cough

teach.model_answer: It is an infection of the lung tissue itself. Air sacs in the affected region fill with fluid and pus, so that part of the lung stops exchanging gas while the rest carries on — which is why findings are often localised to one area rather than heard everywhere. Expect fever and chills, a cough bringing something up, chest discomfort worse on inspiration, and shortness of breath. In an elderly patient the classic picture may be missing entirely: they may simply be confused, weak, not eating, or falling, and pneumonia is a common reason an older person is suddenly not themselves. EMT care is oxygen if needed, position of comfort, and transport.

story.title: Not herself
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 84-year-old female, general weakness, unable to get out of bed.
story.body:
No chest pain. No real complaint of shortness of breath. Her temperature is barely up and she has coughed twice since you arrived.

What her son says is that on Thursday she was doing the crossword and today she does not know what day it is.

In the back of the truck you listen carefully and the right base sounds quite different from the left. The hospital finds pneumonia.

concepts.title: Pulmonary edema and the respiratory face of heart failure
key_points: The left side of the heart fails to move blood forward, so pressure backs up into the lungs
Fluid is pushed out of the capillaries into the alveoli, and gas cannot cross fluid
Crackles, often starting at the bases, and in severe cases pink frothy sputum
Worse lying flat, so the patient sits up; they may report sleeping on several pillows
Look for the other signs of a failing heart: distended neck veins and swollen ankles
CPAP is the intervention that changes these patients, within protocol
This is a heart problem presenting as a breathing problem
misconceptions: Treating it as a lung disease and missing the cardiac cause
Laying the patient flat, which makes it acutely worse
Confusing the crackles of pulmonary edema with the wheeze of asthma without weighing history
exam_favorites: Why it is worse lying flat
Pink frothy sputum
CPAP as the intervention
Neck veins and ankle swelling as supporting signs

read.plain:
This one is a heart problem wearing a lung problem's clothes.

The left side of the heart is meant to push blood out to the body. When it cannot keep up, blood stacks up behind it — into the lungs. Pressure in the lung capillaries rises until fluid is squeezed out of the vessels and into the air sacs themselves. Now the patient has water where air should be, and gas cannot cross water.

You hear it as crackles, usually starting at the bases and climbing as it worsens. In a severe case the patient coughs up pink, frothy sputum — that is fluid and air whipped together with a little blood in it.

Gravity matters here, which is why the history is so useful. Lying flat spreads the fluid across more of the lung, so these patients cannot lie down. Ask how many pillows they sleep on, or whether they have been sleeping in a chair. An answer like 'three pillows, and lately the recliner' is a story of worsening heart failure.

Look for the rest of the picture too: neck veins standing out, ankles and lower legs swollen.

And this is the patient where CPAP earns its place. The pressure holds the air sacs open and helps drive fluid back out of them. Within your protocol, it can turn one of these patients around in front of you.
read.standard: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema results from left ventricular failure, in which inadequate forward output raises left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure until hydrostatic pressure forces fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveolar space, impairing gas exchange. Auscultation reveals crackles, characteristically beginning at the bases and ascending with severity; severe cases produce pink frothy sputum. Symptoms are posture-dependent: recumbency redistributes fluid and worsens dyspnea, producing orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and a history of increasing pillow use or sleeping upright is diagnostically valuable. Associated findings of right-sided congestion include jugular venous distention and dependent peripheral edema. Continuous positive airway pressure is the prehospital intervention of greatest benefit where protocol permits, maintaining alveolar patency and promoting movement of fluid out of the alveolar space.

eli_new.analogy: The pump backed up and flooded the room upstairs. You cannot breathe through a flooded room.
eli_new.body: Think of the heart as a pump in a closed loop. If the pump on the way out of the lungs slows down, everything behind it backs up, and what is directly behind it is the lungs. The fluid in the air sacs did not come from outside. It was squeezed out of the blood vessels by pressure.

teach.prompt: Explain why a failing heart makes someone short of breath, what you would find, and why these patients will not lie down.

must_hit.point: Left heart fails so pressure backs up into the lungs
Fluid is pushed into the air sacs

Worse lying flat, sleeps on pillows or sitting up

teach.model_answer: The left side of the heart cannot move blood forward, so pressure backs up into the lungs until fluid is squeezed out of the capillaries into the air sacs. Gas cannot cross fluid, so the patient becomes hypoxic and short of breath. You hear crackles, typically starting at the bases, and in severe cases they cough up pink frothy sputum. Lying flat spreads that fluid across more lung, so they cannot lie down — ask how many pillows they sleep on or whether they have moved to a chair, because increasing pillows is a story of worsening failure. Look for distended neck veins and swollen ankles too. CPAP is the intervention that changes these patients, within protocol.

story.title: Three pillows and then the chair
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 79-year-old male, difficulty breathing, worse overnight.
story.body:
He is bolt upright on the edge of the bed. There is a wet, bubbling quality to his breathing you can hear from the doorway, and his ankles are swollen over the tops of his slippers.

His wife says he has been on three pillows for a month, and for the last four nights he has slept in the recliner downstairs.

The CPAP goes on in the bedroom. By the time you reach the ambulance he is speaking in whole sentences again.

Wheeze on exhalation leads to asthma, episodic with a known trigger and where a silent chest means worse rather than better, and below it COPD, with a long smoking history, barrel chest and pursed-lip breathing, assessed against the patient's own baseline. concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism
key_points: A clot travels to the lung and blocks blood flow to part of it
That part of the lung is still ventilated but has no blood flowing past it, so air goes in and out for nothing
Classically sudden: one moment fine, the next short of breath
Sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in, and a fast heart rate
Lung sounds are often clear, which is what makes it sneaky
Risk factors matter enormously: recent surgery, immobility, long travel, a known clot in the leg, pregnancy, cancer
There is no EMT treatment beyond oxygen, position and rapid transport
misconceptions: Ruling it out because the lungs sound clear
Ignoring a swollen, painful calf in a breathless patient
Expecting gradual onset
exam_favorites: Sudden onset with clear lung sounds
Risk factor history
Pleuritic pain and tachycardia

read.plain:
A pulmonary embolism is a plumbing problem, not an airway problem. A clot, usually formed in a leg vein, breaks loose, travels up through the heart, and jams in an artery in the lung.

Downstream of that blockage, the lung is still being ventilated perfectly well. Air goes in and out. There is just no blood flowing past to pick the oxygen up. That part of the lung has been disconnected from the circulation.

The onset is the giveaway. Patients describe it as sudden — they were fine, and then they were not. They are short of breath, often with a sharp chest pain that stabs when they breathe in, and their heart is racing.

Here is the trap. When you listen to the chest, it often sounds clear. There is no fluid, no spasm, no infection. A new EMT hears clear lungs and relaxes, which is exactly wrong.

What saves you is the history. Ask what has happened recently. Surgery? A long flight or drive? Bed rest? A leg that has been swollen and sore? Pregnancy, or cancer treatment? Those answers, next to a sudden breathless patient with clear lungs, should worry you a great deal.

There is nothing an EMT can do about the clot. Oxygen, position of comfort, and go.
read.standard: Pulmonary embolism results from occlusion of a pulmonary artery, most often by thrombus originating in the deep veins of the lower extremities. The obstructed segment remains ventilated but is not perfused, creating dead-space ventilation and impairing oxygenation. Presentation is characteristically abrupt, with dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia; auscultation is frequently unremarkable, and clear lung fields do not exclude the diagnosis. Risk assessment is central to recognition and includes recent surgery or immobilisation, prolonged travel, known deep vein thrombosis, malignancy, pregnancy and hormonal therapy. Prehospital management at the EMT level is limited to supplemental oxygen, position of comfort and expedited transport; definitive management is in hospital.

eli_new.analogy: The hallway is open and the door is open, but the delivery truck cannot get down the street.
eli_new.body: Everything you have learned about breathing problems is about air not getting in. This one is about blood not getting there. The air arrives exactly as it should and finds nobody home to collect it, which is why the lungs can sound completely normal while the patient is in serious trouble.

teach.prompt: Explain what a pulmonary embolism actually is, why the lungs can sound clear, and what in the history would raise your suspicion.

must_hit.point: A clot blocks blood flow to part of the lung
That lung is ventilated but not perfused
Sudden onset, pleuritic pain, fast heart rate
Lungs often sound clear
Risk factors: surgery, immobility, travel, leg clot, pregnancy, cancer

teach.model_answer: A clot, usually from a leg vein, travels to the lung and blocks an artery there. The lung beyond it is still being ventilated but has no blood flowing past, so the air goes in and out for nothing. It comes on suddenly — fine one minute, not the next — with shortness of breath, often a sharp pain that is worse on breathing in, and a fast heart rate. The trap is that the lungs frequently sound completely clear, so clear lungs must not reassure you. What raises suspicion is the history: recent surgery, immobility or bed rest, a long flight or drive, a swollen painful calf, pregnancy, or cancer. There is no EMT treatment for the clot — oxygen, position of comfort and rapid transport.

story.title: Clear lungs, terrible patient
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 46-year-old female, sudden shortness of breath, office building.
story.body:
She is pale, breathing fast, and says it started twenty minutes ago out of nowhere. Sharp pain on the right when she breathes in. Heart rate high.

You listen and the chest is clear. Genuinely clear, both sides. The new EMT visibly relaxes.

Then you ask what she has been doing. She flew back from Australia four days ago, and her right calf has been sore and swollen since.

You stop relaxing.
