concepts.title: Spontaneous pneumothorax
key_points: Air escapes from the lung into the space between the lung and the chest wall, and the lung collapses inward
Spontaneous means it happened without trauma
Classically a tall, thin, young person, often a smoker, sometimes during exertion
Sudden sharp chest pain on one side with shortness of breath
Breath sounds are reduced or absent on the affected side
Watch for it getting worse: rising distress, a falling blood pressure and a deviating trachea suggest a tension pneumothorax, which is an emergency
misconceptions: Expecting trauma to be involved
Missing a one-sided difference in breath sounds
Failing to recognise progression to tension
exam_favorites: One-sided decreased breath sounds
The classic patient description
Recognising progression to tension pneumothorax

read.plain:
The lung does not float free in the chest. It is held expanded against the chest wall by a vacuum in the thin space between two membranes. Break that seal and the lung's own elasticity pulls it inward, away from the wall. It collapses.

Spontaneous means nobody hit them. A weak spot on the lung surface gives way on its own, often in a tall, thin young person, often a smoker, sometimes during exertion or even at rest.

They will describe it as sudden: a sharp pain on one side of the chest and shortness of breath that started in an instant.

The finding to look for is asymmetry. Listen on both sides at the same level. If one side is noticeably quieter than the other, that means something.

Now the part that matters most. Sometimes air keeps entering that space with each breath and cannot escape. Pressure builds, pushing on the lung, the heart and the great vessels. The patient becomes rapidly worse: severe distress, falling blood pressure, distended neck veins, and eventually a trachea pushed away from the affected side. That is a tension pneumothorax, and it needs decompression now. Recognise it, call for ALS, and move.
read.standard: Pneumothorax is the presence of air within the pleural space, abolishing the negative pressure that maintains lung expansion and permitting collapse of the affected lung by elastic recoil. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without trauma, typically from rupture of a subpleural bleb, and classically affects tall, thin young adults, with smoking as a significant risk factor; onset may occur at rest or during exertion. Presentation comprises sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, with diminished or absent breath sounds over the affected hemithorax. Progression to tension pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space without escape, producing progressive intrapleural pressure elevation with mediastinal shift, impaired venous return and hemodynamic collapse; signs include severe respiratory distress, hypotension, jugular venous distention and, as a late finding, tracheal deviation away from the affected side. Tension pneumothorax requires immediate decompression.

eli_new.analogy: The lung is held open by suction, like a suction cup on glass. Let air in behind it and it peels off and shrinks.
eli_new.body: People assume a collapsed lung means something crushed it. It is the opposite. The lung is naturally elastic and wants to shrink; what keeps it open is the vacuum holding it against the chest wall. Break the vacuum and it does what it always wanted to do.

teach.prompt: Explain what a spontaneous pneumothorax is, who classically gets one, and what would tell you it is becoming a tension pneumothorax.

must_hit.point: Air in the space around the lung so it collapses
No trauma involved
Classically tall, thin, young, often a smoker
Decreased breath sounds on one side
Tension: worsening distress, falling BP, tracheal deviation

teach.model_answer: Air gets into the space between the lung and the chest wall, the vacuum that holds the lung expanded is lost, and the lung's own elasticity pulls it inward so it collapses. Spontaneous means it happened without any trauma — classically a tall, thin young person, often a smoker. They describe sudden sharp pain on one side with shortness of breath. Listen at the same level on both sides: decreased or absent sounds on one side is your finding. If air keeps entering and cannot escape, pressure builds into a tension pneumothorax — rapidly worsening distress, falling blood pressure, distended neck veins, and as a late sign the trachea pushed away from the affected side. That needs decompression immediately, so call for ALS and move.

story.title: Halfway through a set
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 22-year-old male, chest pain and shortness of breath, gym.
story.body:
He is tall, thin, and was on the bench press when it happened. Sharp pain on the left, instantly, and he could not get a full breath.

No impact, no injury, nobody dropped anything on him. You listen: the right side sounds normal and the left is noticeably quieter.

On the way in you check it again every few minutes, watching his pressure and his neck veins, because the thing you are really watching for is it getting worse.

concepts.title: Hyperventilation syndrome
key_points: Breathing faster and deeper than the body needs, driving carbon dioxide down
Low carbon dioxide causes tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, light-headedness, and spasm of the hands and feet
It is a diagnosis of exclusion and must never be the first thing you assume
Serious causes of fast breathing include pulmonary embolism, diabetic emergencies, sepsis, poisoning and hypoxia
Do not have the patient breathe into a paper bag
Coach the breathing rate down, give oxygen if there is any doubt, and transport
misconceptions: Diagnosing anxiety at the door and missing a pulmonary embolism or a diabetic emergency
Using a paper bag
Withholding oxygen because it is 'just anxiety'
exam_favorites: That it is a diagnosis of exclusion
No paper bag
The dangerous causes of rapid breathing

read.plain:
A patient breathing far faster and deeper than their body requires blows off too much carbon dioxide. That change in blood chemistry produces a very specific and frightening set of symptoms: tingling around the lips and in the fingertips, light-headedness, a sense of not being able to get enough air, and in a bad episode, cramping spasm of the hands and feet.

Those symptoms feel exactly like something catastrophic, which makes the patient breathe faster still.

Now the warning, and it is the most important thing in this concept. Fast breathing is a symptom, not a diagnosis. A patient breathing fast may have a clot in their lung, may be in a diabetic crisis, may be septic, may be poisoned, may simply be hypoxic. All of those look like 'anxious and breathing fast' from the doorway.

So hyperventilation syndrome is what you are left with when the dangerous things have been considered and do not fit. It is never the first thing you decide.

And do not use a paper bag. That practice is out, and it has killed people whose fast breathing was hypoxia.

What works is your voice. Sit with them, get eye contact, and coach the rate down slowly. Give oxygen if there is any doubt at all, and transport.
read.standard: Hyperventilation syndrome describes minute ventilation in excess of metabolic requirement, producing hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis. Resulting symptoms include perioral and digital paresthesia, light-headedness, subjective air hunger and, in marked cases, carpopedal spasm; these symptoms are themselves anxiogenic and may perpetuate the cycle. Critically, the condition is a diagnosis of exclusion. Tachypnea is a nonspecific sign, and organic causes including pulmonary embolism, diabetic ketoacidosis, sepsis, toxic ingestion and hypoxia must be considered before attributing rapid breathing to anxiety. Rebreathing into a paper bag is no longer practised and is potentially lethal where the underlying cause is hypoxia. Management comprises reassurance, verbal coaching of respiratory rate, supplemental oxygen where any doubt exists, and transport.

eli_new.analogy: Fast breathing is a fire alarm. You do not switch off the alarm before finding out whether there is a fire.
eli_new.body: The symptoms of blowing off too much carbon dioxide are dramatic and completely real. The danger is not the symptoms; it is the assumption. Deciding 'this is just anxiety' at the front door is how a clot in the lung or a diabetic emergency gets missed.

teach.prompt: Explain why hyperventilation syndrome is a diagnosis you should be reluctant to make, and what you actually do for the patient.

must_hit.point: Low carbon dioxide causes tingling, light-headedness, hand and foot spasm
It is a diagnosis of exclusion
Dangerous causes include PE, diabetic emergencies, sepsis, poisoning, hypoxia
No paper bag
Coach the rate down, give oxygen if in doubt

teach.model_answer: Breathing faster and deeper than the body needs drives carbon dioxide down, which causes tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, light-headedness, a feeling of air hunger and sometimes cramping spasm of the hands and feet. Those symptoms are frightening, so the patient breathes faster still. The reason to be reluctant is that fast breathing is a symptom, not a diagnosis — a pulmonary embolism, a diabetic crisis, sepsis, a poisoning or plain hypoxia all present as someone anxious and breathing fast. So this is what you are left with after the dangerous things do not fit, never your opening assumption. Do not use a paper bag; that is out and it has killed hypoxic patients. Sit with them, coach the rate down with your voice, give oxygen if there is any doubt, and transport.

story.title: Not just a panic attack
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 34-year-old female, panic attack, called by a coworker.
story.body:
The call came in as a panic attack and she looks the part: breathing fast, hands cramping, tingling in her fingers, frightened.

Your partner starts coaching her breathing, which is right. You start asking questions, which is also right.

She had a caesarean eleven days ago. Her left leg has been sore. Nothing about her chest sounds wrong at all.

You put oxygen on her and you do not write 'anxiety' on anything.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis and croup
key_points: Both cause noisy breathing in a child, and telling them apart changes what you do
Croup is viral, comes on over days, is worse at night, and produces a harsh barking cough with stridor
Epiglottitis is a rapidly progressing infection of the epiglottis itself and is a true emergency
The epiglottitis picture: sudden high fever, drooling because swallowing hurts, a muffled voice, and a child sitting forward refusing to lie down
Do not put anything in the mouth of a suspected epiglottitis patient and do not try to look at the throat
Keep the child calm and with a parent; distress can worsen the obstruction
Give oxygen in whatever way the child will tolerate and transport without agitating them
misconceptions: Inspecting the throat of a child with suspected epiglottitis
Separating a frightened child from a parent
Treating every stridulous child as croup
Forcing a mask onto a child who is fighting it
exam_favorites: Drooling, muffled voice and tripoding as the epiglottitis picture
Barking cough and night-time worsening as croup
Never inspect the airway
Keeping the child calm as a treatment in itself

read.plain:
Two childhood illnesses, both noisy, and the difference matters.

Croup is the common one. It is viral, builds over a day or two, and is usually worse at night. The sound is unmistakable once you have heard it: a harsh, barking cough like a seal, with stridor when they breathe in. The child is unwell but usually still drinking, still talking, still themselves.

Epiglottitis is the one that frightens experienced people. The epiglottis itself becomes infected and swells, and it sits right at the entrance to the airway. It moves fast. The child has a sudden high fever, is drooling because swallowing hurts too much, has a muffled voice rather than a barking cough, and is sitting bolt upright leaning forward, refusing to lie down. They look frightened and unwell in a way croup children usually do not.

Here is the rule that matters. Do not put anything in that child's mouth. No tongue depressor, no look at the throat, no thermometer. A swollen epiglottis can be tipped into complete obstruction by that kind of stimulation.

Keep the child calm. Leave them in whatever position they have chosen. Keep the parent with them, and let the parent hold the oxygen if that is what the child will accept. Crying and struggling make the obstruction worse, so calm is not a comfort measure here, it is treatment.

Then go, gently, and let the hospital know what is coming.
read.standard: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a viral illness of the subglottic airway with gradual onset over one to two days, characteristic nocturnal exacerbation, a barking cough and inspiratory stridor; children typically remain interactive and able to swallow. Epiglottitis is bacterial infection and inflammation of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures, characterised by abrupt onset, high fever, drooling secondary to odynophagia, muffled voice, tripod positioning and severe anxiety, and carries a risk of rapid progression to complete airway obstruction. Examination of the oropharynx, including use of a tongue depressor, is contraindicated in suspected epiglottitis, as stimulation may precipitate complete obstruction. Management comprises minimising distress, permitting the child to maintain their position of choice, keeping the caregiver present, delivering oxygen in whatever form is tolerated, avoiding agitation, and expedited transport with hospital notification.

eli_new.analogy: The epiglottis is the lid over the windpipe. If the lid swells, do not go poking at it.
eli_new.body: Both children make noise when they breathe, which is why they get confused. The differences are in the details: croup coughs like a seal and comes on slowly; epiglottitis drools, speaks in a muffled voice, and got sick fast. And the single thing to remember is that you never look in the throat of the second one.

teach.prompt: Explain how you would tell croup from epiglottitis in a child, and what you must not do if you suspect epiglottitis.

must_hit.point: Croup: barking cough, stridor, gradual, worse at night
Epiglottitis: sudden high fever, drooling, muffled voice, sitting forward
Never inspect the throat or put anything in the mouth
Keep the child calm and with a parent

teach.model_answer: Croup is viral, builds over a day or two, is worse at night, and gives a harsh barking cough with stridor in a child who is generally still interactive and swallowing. Epiglottitis comes on fast with a high fever, the child drools because swallowing hurts, the voice is muffled rather than barking, and they sit bolt upright leaning forward and will not lie down. If you suspect epiglottitis, you must not put anything in the mouth — no tongue depressor, no throat inspection — because stimulating a swollen epiglottis can tip it into complete obstruction. Keep the child calm in whatever position they have chosen, keep the parent with them, let the parent hold the oxygen if that is what is tolerated, and transport gently with early notification.

story.title: Let her hold it
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — four-year-old, difficulty breathing, parents very worried.
story.body:
She is on her mother's lap, leaning forward, drooling onto a towel. Her voice is thick and quiet when she answers. She got sick this afternoon and has a high fever.

The new EMT reaches for a penlight and you stop his hand.

You give her mother the oxygen tubing to hold near her face, tell her to keep doing exactly what she is doing, and you carry them both out together. Nobody raises their voice. Nobody lies her down.

concepts.title: Infectious respiratory disease: precautions and awareness
key_points: Pertussis, RSV, influenza and COVID all spread through the respiratory route
Standard precautions apply to every patient; respiratory illness adds eye protection and a mask
A mask on the patient, where tolerated, reduces spread at the source
Pertussis causes violent coughing fits, and in children a whooping sound on breathing in afterward
RSV is a major cause of respiratory distress in infants and can be severe in the very young
Influenza and COVID cover a wide range from mild illness to respiratory failure
Exposures are reported and documented through your service's process
misconceptions: Using standard precautions only after the patient looks infectious

exam_favorites: Precautions applied before assessment, not after
Masking the patient at the source
RSV in infants
Reporting exposures

read.plain:
You will meet respiratory infections constantly, and most of the time you will not know which one you have until long after the call.

That is the whole argument for doing the same thing every time. Standard precautions on every patient, and for anybody with a cough or a fever, add eye protection and a mask for yourself. If the patient will tolerate a mask, putting one on them stops a great deal at the source, which is more effective than anything you do at your own end.

A few worth knowing by name. Pertussis, whooping cough, causes fits of coughing so violent the patient cannot breathe between them, and in a child the desperate breath afterward makes the whoop. RSV is a common cause of infants in real respiratory distress, and small infants have very little reserve. Influenza and COVID both run from mild to life-threatening, and neither announces which it is going to be at the door.

And if you are exposed, report it through your service's process and document it. That is not paperwork for its own sake; it is what makes follow-up and treatment possible.
read.standard: Respiratory infectious diseases encountered in EMS include pertussis, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza and COVID-19, all transmitted by respiratory routes. Standard precautions are applied to every patient contact irrespective of presentation, with the addition of eye protection and a respiratory mask for patients with cough or fever; source control by masking the patient where tolerated is more effective than provider protection alone. Pertussis produces paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop in children. RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis and severe respiratory distress in infants, who possess limited respiratory reserve. Influenza and COVID-19 span a spectrum from mild illness to respiratory failure. Occupational exposures must be reported and documented through the service's exposure control process to enable follow-up and post-exposure management.

eli_new.analogy: You do not put on a seatbelt once you see the other car.
eli_new.body: The reason precautions are 'standard' is that you cannot tell by looking. By the time a patient looks obviously infectious, you have already been breathing the same air for ten minutes. Doing it the same way every time is the only version that works.

teach.prompt: Explain what precautions you take with a coughing, feverish patient and why you take them before you know what is wrong.

teach.model_answer: Standard precautions go on every patient, before you know anything. For anyone coughing or febrile, add eye protection and a mask for yourself, and if they will tolerate it, put a mask on the patient too — stopping it at the source does more than protecting your own face. You do it before you know what is wrong because you usually never find out on scene, and by the time someone looks infectious you have already shared their air. Worth knowing by name: pertussis with its violent coughing fits and whoop in children, RSV which puts infants into real distress, and influenza and COVID which both run from mild to life-threatening. If you are exposed, report and document it through your service's process so follow-up can happen.

story.title: Nobody said anything about a cough
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 30-year-old male, abdominal pain, residence.
story.body:
Dispatched for abdominal pain. No mention of anything respiratory.

He coughed twice while you were taking his history, said it was nothing, and mentioned his daughter had been off school all week.

You had gloves and glasses on from the doorway because that is what you always do. Three days later the service told you the family had tested positive for influenza.

The habit is the only part of that you controlled.

concepts.title: Assisting with an MDI and a small-volume nebulizer
key_points: The EMT assists a patient with their own prescribed medication, within protocol and often with medical direction
A metered-dose inhaler delivers a measured puff that the patient must time with their own breath
A spacer holds the puff so the timing matters less; it is especially useful for children and for the very breathless
A small-volume nebulizer turns liquid medication into a mist driven by oxygen, breathed in over several minutes
A nebulizer needs no coordination, which is why it suits a patient too breathless to time a puff
Check the six rights before assisting, and confirm the medication is prescribed to this patient and is not expired
Reassess after: breath sounds, work of breathing, speech and vital signs
misconceptions: Assisting with a medication prescribed to somebody else
Expecting a severely breathless patient to coordinate an inhaler without a spacer
Giving the dose and not reassessing
Skipping the expiry check
exam_favorites: The six rights
Spacer use and why
Nebulizer versus MDI in a very breathless patient
Reassessment after assisting

read.plain:
An EMT does not carry these medications. What an EMT does is help a patient take their own, within protocol, usually after contacting medical direction.

A metered-dose inhaler is the small pressurised canister. One press delivers one measured puff, and the patient has to breathe in slowly at the same moment. That coordination is harder than it sounds, and it is hardest for exactly the patients who need it most.

That is what a spacer is for. It is a chamber between the inhaler and the mouth. The puff goes into the chamber and hangs there, so the patient can breathe it in over a few breaths instead of catching it in one. Use one for children, and for anyone too breathless to coordinate.

A small-volume nebulizer is the other route. Liquid medication sits in a cup, oxygen flows through it, and it comes out as a mist the patient breathes over several minutes through a mask or mouthpiece. There is nothing to coordinate — they just breathe. That makes it the better choice for someone who is really struggling.

Before you assist with anything, run the six rights: right patient, right medication, right dose, right route, right time, right documentation. Check that it is this patient's own prescription and that it is in date. Both of those get missed.

And afterwards, go back and look. Listen to the chest again, watch the work of breathing, see whether they can get more words out, and take another set of vitals. If nothing changed, that is information too.
read.standard: At the EMT level, bronchodilator administration consists of assisting the patient with their own prescribed medication under protocol, commonly with online medical direction. A metered-dose inhaler delivers a fixed-volume aerosolised dose that requires coordination between actuation and slow inspiration; a valved holding chamber or spacer suspends the dose, removing the coordination requirement and improving delivery, and is particularly indicated in pediatric patients and in patients with severe dyspnea. A small-volume nebulizer aerosolises liquid medication using an oxygen flow, delivered over several minutes by mask or mouthpiece, requiring no inspiratory coordination and therefore suited to the severely dyspneic patient. Prior to assisting, the six rights are confirmed, together with verification that the medication is prescribed to that patient and is within its expiry date. Post-administration reassessment includes breath sounds, work of breathing, ability to speak and vital signs.

eli_new.analogy: An inhaler is a dart you have to catch in mid-air. A spacer is a bucket you can scoop it out of.
eli_new.body: The hardest part of an inhaler is not the drug, it is the timing. Press and breathe in at exactly the same moment, slowly. Somebody gasping for air cannot do that, so the puff ends up on the back of their throat. A spacer catches it and lets them take it over several ordinary breaths, and a nebulizer removes the problem completely.

teach.model_answer: You are helping the patient take their own prescribed medication, within protocol and usually after contacting medical direction. An inhaler delivers one measured puff and the patient has to breathe in slowly at exactly that moment, which is hardest for the patients who need it most — a spacer fixes that by holding the puff in a chamber so they can take it over several breaths, and it is especially useful for children and for anyone very breathless. A nebulizer turns liquid medication into a mist driven by oxygen over several minutes, with nothing to coordinate, so it suits someone really struggling. Before assisting, run the six rights and specifically confirm it is this patient's own prescription and that it has not expired. Afterwards, reassess: breath sounds, work of breathing, how many words they can manage, and another set of vitals.

story.title: The puff that went nowhere
story.dispatch: Rescue 2 — 9-year-old, asthma attack, school nurse's office.
story.body:
He has his own inhaler and the nurse has already helped him with two puffs. He is still working hard and you can hear him from across the room.

Watching him try again, you see it: he presses, and breathes in about half a second later. The puff hits the back of his throat and stops there.

There is a spacer in the side pocket of his bag, unused. With the spacer on, he takes the same medication over four ordinary breaths, and this time you can hear it reach where it was meant to go.
